a: A process is an independent running program with its own memory space. It is isolated, so a crash in one process doesn't directly corrupt another. A thread is a unit of execution within a process, sharing that process's memory with other threads in it. Threads are cheaper to create and switch than processes, but shared memory means threads can step on each other's data without synchronization.
topics.example:
Process (own memory space, PID)
 ├── Thread 1 (main)
 ├── Thread 2
 └── Thread 3   ← all share the process's memory

A web server process handles many requests using a pool of threads: all threads share the same loaded application code/memory (fast to spin up), but a shared in-memory counter accessed by two threads at once needs a lock or it'll be corrupted.

Python:
  multiprocessing.Process(target=crunch).start() # process: own memory, true parallelism
  threading.Thread(target=fetch).start()         # thread: shared memory, GIL caps CPU work

Go:
  exec.Command("worker").Start()    // separate OS process, isolated memory
  go handle(req)                    // goroutine: runtime-managed, shared memory

Real world: Chrome runs every tab as its own process, so one crashed tab never kills the browser. Gunicorn: -w 4 --threads 2 = 4 processes × 2 threads = 8 concurrent requests. PostgreSQL spawns one process per connection: that is exactly why max_connections stays small and PgBouncer exists.

a: Concurrency: multiple tasks making progress over the same time period. It can happen on a single core via time-slicing: fast task switching gives the illusion of 'at once'. Parallelism: multiple tasks literally executing at the exact same instant, which requires multiple cores. Concurrency is about structure (how you design the program), parallelism is about execution (whether it actually runs simultaneously).
topics.example:
Concurrency (1 core, tasks take turns)
 Task A: ██░░██░░██   (░ = waiting on I/O)
 Task B: ░░██░░██░░   ← B runs while A waits, not after A finishes

Parallelism (2+ cores, same instant)
 Core 1: Task A ██████████
 Core 2: Task B ██████████

Python:
  asyncio.gather(fetch_a(), fetch_b())       # concurrency: one thread interleaves I/O waits
  ProcessPoolExecutor().map(resize, images)  # parallelism: one process per core

Go:
  go fetchA(); go fetchB()   // concurrency: goroutines interleave on few OS threads
  runtime.GOMAXPROCS(8)      // parallelism cap: up to 8 cores execute at once

Real world: a download manager (IDM) downloads 5 files 'at once' on one core: each download mostly waits on the network, so the CPU switches to whichever file has bytes ready (concurrency). Node.js serves thousands of requests the same way. But 5 video encodes on one core fight for the CPU: that needs real cores (parallelism). Rule: I/O-bound wants concurrency, CPU-bound wants parallelism.

a: Mutex (mutual exclusion lock): binary, owned by whoever locked it. Only the locking thread can unlock it. It protects a critical section so only one thread touches a shared resource at a time. Semaphore: a counter allowing up to N holders at once, not tied to a single owner. It limits concurrent access to a pool of N resources (for example N DB connections).
topics.example:
Mutex (1 key)                 Semaphore (count = 3)
 T1 ██ holds lock, works       T1 T2 T3 ██ all inside
 T2 ░░ waits for unlock        T4 ░░ waits for a free slot

Python:
  with threading.Lock(): counter += 1        # mutex: one thread at a time
  with threading.Semaphore(3): call_api()    # semaphore: at most 3 at once

Go:
  mu.Lock(); counter++; mu.Unlock()   // sync.Mutex: one goroutine at a time
  sem := make(chan struct{}, 3)       // buffered channel = semaphore of 3

Real world: mutex is a cafe toilet key: one key, one person inside, next waits. Semaphore is a parking lot with 3 spaces: 3 cars in, car 4 waits until one leaves. In code: a DB connection pool of size 10 is a semaphore (at most 10 borrowers). A Postgres row lock during UPDATE acts like a mutex on that row.

a: Deadlock: two or more threads or processes each wait on a resource the other holds, so none can proceed. It needs 4 conditions at the same time (Coffman conditions): mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption, circular wait. Break any one to prevent deadlock. Easiest fix in practice: kill circular wait by always acquiring locks in a fixed order.
topics.example:
T1 holds Lock A ──wants──▶ Lock B (held by T2)
T2 holds Lock B ──wants──▶ Lock A (held by T1)
        both wait forever (circular wait)

Python:
  with lock_a:
      with lock_b: transfer()   # every thread locks A then B: fixed order, no cycle

Go:
  muA.Lock(); muB.Lock()   // same order in every goroutine breaks circular wait

Real world: two bank transfers, X sends to Y while Y sends to X. Each locks its own account first then wants the other: frozen. Fix: always lock the lower account id first. Postgres detects this and kills one transaction with 'deadlock detected'. Two people in a narrow doorway each waiting for the other to pass: same picture.

a: A race condition happens when the result depends on the unpredictable timing or order of concurrent operations, usually unsynchronized access to shared state. The classic shape is read-modify-write on shared data without protection. It can pass every test and fail rarely in production under real load, which makes it notoriously hard to debug.
topics.example:
counter = 5
 T1: read 5 ─▶ +1 ─▶ write 6
 T2: read 5 ────▶ +1 ─▶ write 6   ← one increment lost (should be 7)

Python:
  counter += 1               # read-modify-write: 3 steps, racy
  with lock: counter += 1    # lock makes it one atomic step

Go:
  counter++                      // racy across goroutines (go test -race catches it)
  atomic.AddInt64(&counter, 1)   // atomic op: safe without a lock

Real world: two buyers grab the last ticket at the same moment, both see '1 left', both pay, event oversold. Fix in SQL: UPDATE stock SET qty = qty - 1 WHERE qty > 0 (the DB does read-modify-write atomically). Like counters on posts lose likes the same way without atomic increments.

a: Stack: fast fixed-size memory for function calls and local variables. LIFO: each call pushes a frame, each return pops it, so freeing is automatic and instant. Heap: larger memory for dynamic or long-lived data. Allocation costs more and something must free it: manually (C) or a garbage collector.

Garbage collection (Go, Java, JS, Python) reclaims heap memory no longer reachable from the program. It trades some runtime overhead and pause time for killing most manual memory bugs (use-after-free, double-free). GC does not stop leaks: keep a reference forever and the object never dies.
topics.example:
Stack (per call, auto-freed)    Heap (shared, GC-managed)
 │ parse()  │ ◀ push on call     objects that outlive the call
 │ handle() │   pop on return    freed when nothing points to them
 │ main()   │

Python:
  def f(): x = len(items)    # frame + locals: stack, gone on return
  cache = load_users()       # big object: heap, GC frees when unreachable

Go:
  x := 42                            // stays on stack: freed on return
  func g() *User { u := User{}; return &u }  // u escapes to heap, GC frees later

Real world: recursion with no base case overflows the stack (each call adds a frame). A global map used as a cache with no eviction grows forever: classic leak even with GC. Go escape analysis decides stack vs heap at compile time: go build -gcflags='-m' shows what escapes.

a: When the CPU switches from one thread or process to another, it saves the current state (registers, program counter) and loads the next one's. That overhead is a context switch. It also cools the CPU cache, so the real cost is bigger than the save/load itself. Too many threads on too few cores means the CPU spends time switching instead of working.
topics.example:
Core: [T1 run] save T1 ▶ load T2 [T2 run] save T2 ▶ load T1 ...
               └── switch cost: registers + program counter, cache goes cold

Python:
  for t in threads: t.start()     # 1000 OS threads: kernel switches, expensive
  await asyncio.gather(*tasks)    # task switch in user space: no kernel cost

Go:
  go handle(conn)   // goroutine switch: Go scheduler, user space, ~100ns
                    // OS thread switch: kernel, ~1-10µs plus cold cache

Real world: Apache thread-per-connection dies at 10K connections partly from switch overhead. Nginx and Node.js use one event loop per core instead: few threads, no switch storm. Go multiplexes millions of goroutines onto a few OS threads (M:N scheduling) for the same reason.

a: TCP: connection-oriented. Handshake, acknowledgements and retransmission give ordered reliable delivery. Use when correctness beats raw speed (HTTP, databases). UDP: connectionless. No delivery guarantee, no ordering, but lower overhead and latency. Use when speed beats occasional loss (video calls, DNS, gaming, metrics).
topics.example:
TCP: SYN ─▶ SYN-ACK ─▶ ACK, then data + ACKs (lost packet resent)
UDP: send ─▶ send ─▶ send (no handshake, no resend, no order)

Python:
  socket.socket(AF_INET, SOCK_STREAM)  # TCP: reliable stream
  socket.socket(AF_INET, SOCK_DGRAM)   # UDP: datagrams, best effort

Go:
  net.Dial("tcp", addr)   // handshake, ordered stream
  net.Dial("udp", addr)   // just send, no guarantees

Real world: video call uses UDP: a dropped frame is a brief glitch, retransmitting it would cause stutter. File download uses TCP: every byte must arrive in order or the file is corrupt. DNS uses UDP for speed with TCP fallback for big responses.

a: HTTP is stateless request/response over TCP. HTTPS = HTTP over TLS, which adds encryption, integrity and server authentication (via certificates).

TLS handshake (simplified): client hello (supported ciphers) → server hello + certificate → key exchange derives a shared symmetric session key → both sides switch to encrypted traffic with that key. Asymmetric crypto is used only up front to exchange the key: too slow for bulk data.
topics.example:
Client                          Server
  ── ClientHello (ciphers) ────▶
  ◀── ServerHello + cert ───────
  ── key exchange ─────────────▶   both derive session key
  ════ all traffic encrypted with symmetric key ════

Inspect it:
  curl -v https://bank.com                  # prints handshake + cert check
  openssl s_client -connect bank.com:443    # shows certificate chain

Real world: the browser padlock means the cert is signed by a trusted CA and matches the domain. TLS 1.3 cut the handshake to 1 round trip. Load balancers often terminate TLS so backend services speak plain HTTP inside the network.

a: REST: resource URLs + HTTP verbs. Simple, cacheable, widely understood. Weakness: over-fetching or under-fetching and extra round trips for related resources. GraphQL: client asks for exactly the fields it needs in one query. Solves over/under-fetching but is harder to cache and naive resolvers hide N+1 queries. gRPC: binary Protobuf over HTTP/2. Strongly typed contracts, very fast, supports streaming. Great for internal service-to-service calls, less natural for public browser APIs.
topics.example:
REST:    GET /users/1  then  GET /users/1/orders     (2 round trips)
GraphQL: query { user(id:1){ name orders{ total } } } (1 trip, exact fields)
gRPC:    rpc GetUser(UserRequest) returns (User)      (binary, typed, HTTP/2)

Real world: public API for third-party developers → REST (familiar, cacheable). Mobile screen needing user + last 5 orders + reviews in one trip → GraphQL. orders-service calling inventory-service thousands of times per second → gRPC.

a: A load balancer spreads traffic across backend instances for availability and scale. L4 (transport layer): routes by IP and port only. Fast, protocol-agnostic, cannot see HTTP. L7 (application layer): routes by HTTP content (path, host, headers). Enables smart routing and TLS termination.
Common algorithms: round robin, least connections, weighted (bigger instance gets more), consistent hashing (same key hits the same backend, good for caching).
topics.example:
┌─▶ api-1
client ─▶ LB ├─▶ api-2    L4: picks backend by IP:port only
            └─▶ api-3    L7: reads request, /api ─▶ API, /static ─▶ CDN

Nginx (L7):
  upstream api { least_conn; server api1:8080; server api2:8080; }
  location /api/ { proxy_pass http://api; }   # path-based routing

Real world: AWS NLB is L4, ALB is L7. Nginx and HAProxy do L7 routing plus TLS termination so backends speak plain HTTP. Kubernetes: Service is L4, Ingress is L7.

a: DNS translates a human-readable domain into an IP address. Simplified lookup path: browser cache → OS cache → recursive resolver (often your ISP or 8.8.8.8) → root nameserver → TLD nameserver (.com) → authoritative nameserver for the domain, which returns the IP. Results are cached at each layer according to TTL.
topics.example:
browser cache ─▶ OS cache ─▶ recursive resolver (8.8.8.8)
                              │ root:  'ask the .com servers'
                              │ .com:  'ask ns1.example.com'
                              └ authoritative: api.example.com = 1.2.3.4 (TTL 300)

Inspect it:
  dig api.example.com          # answer + remaining TTL
  dig +trace api.example.com   # walks root → TLD → authoritative

Real world: TTL 300 means an IP change takes up to 5 minutes to reach everyone, so teams lower TTL before a migration. Route 53 and Cloudflare DNS are authoritative nameservers. 8.8.8.8 and 1.1.1.1 are recursive resolvers.

a: A Content Delivery Network caches static (and sometimes dynamic) content on edge servers close to users, cutting latency and offloading the origin. Cache behavior is controlled by headers (Cache-Control, ETag) and caches can be purged on deploy.
topics.example:
user (Dhaka) ─▶ edge (Singapore) ── cache hit: ~30ms, done
                      │ cache miss
                      └─▶ origin (US) ~250ms, edge keeps a copy

Headers:
  Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable   # hashed bundle: cache 1 year
  ETag: "abc123"   # revalidate: 304 Not Modified if unchanged

Real world: Cloudflare and CloudFront serve from hundreds of edge locations. Deploys avoid stale files by hashing names (app.9f3c.js): new name, new cache entry. Netflix ships edge boxes inside ISPs (Open Connect) so video never crosses the ocean.

a: Rate limiting protects an API from abuse or buggy clients by capping requests per client over a time window. Common algorithms: token bucket and sliding window. State usually lives in Redis so all instances share the counts.

Versioning lets an API evolve without breaking existing clients: URL (/v1/users), header (Accept: application/vnd.api.v2+json) or query param. Prefer additive backward-compatible changes. Reserve a new version for breaking changes.
topics.example:
Token bucket (cap 10, refill 1 per 6s)
  request takes 1 token: ●●●●●●●○○○
  bucket empty ─▶ 429 Too Many Requests + Retry-After: 30

Redis fixed window:
  INCR rate:user42:1712        # count this minute's window
  EXPIRE rate:user42:1712 60   # window dies after 60s

Real world: GitHub API allows 5000 requests/hour and returns X-RateLimit-Remaining headers. Stripe versions by date header (Stripe-Version: 2024-06-20) so old integrations never break. /v1/orders keeps its shape while /v2/orders changes fields.

a: Polling: client asks 'anything new?' on an interval. Simple but wasteful and updates arrive late. Long polling: server holds the request open until it has data, then the client immediately reopens. Less waste, still one request per message. WebSockets: one persistent full-duplex connection. Server pushes instantly with no per-message HTTP overhead. Ideal for chat, live dashboards, notifications.
topics.example:
Polling:    req ▶ empty   req ▶ empty   req ▶ data!   (waste + delay)
Long poll:  req ▶ ........... data!   req ▶ ......
WebSocket:  ══ connect once ══ msg ◀─▶ msg ◀─▶ msg   (both ways, instant)

Python:
  await ws.send_json(update)   # server pushes, no request needed

Go:
  conn, _ := upgrader.Upgrade(w, r, nil)   // HTTP connection upgrades to WebSocket

Real world: Slack and WhatsApp Web hold one WebSocket per client for instant messages. Stock tickers and live dashboards push over WebSockets. Old corporate proxies sometimes block them, so libraries like Socket.IO fall back to long polling.

a: Normalization removes duplicate data by splitting tables so each fact lives in exactly one place.

1NF: every column holds a single atomic value, no repeating groups. 2NF: 1NF + every non-key column depends on the WHOLE primary key (matters for composite keys). 3NF: 2NF + no non-key column depends on another non-key column (no transitive dependency). BCNF: a stricter 3NF for edge cases with overlapping candidate keys.
In interviews: denormalization is a valid trade-off for read-heavy systems. Say so, don't just recite the forms.
topics.example:
Bad (violates 2NF):
 orders(order_id, product_id, product_name, qty)
                              └ depends on product_id only, not the full key

Fixed:
 orders(order_id, product_id, qty)
 products(product_id, product_name)   ← each fact lives once

Real world: rename a product in the normalized schema = 1 row update. In the bad schema = millions of order rows to fix (and some get missed: inconsistent data). Analytics warehouses denormalize on purpose (star schema) to skip joins on read-heavy queries.

a: ACID is what a database transaction guarantees so your data stays correct even under failures or concurrent access.

Atomicity: all steps in a transaction succeed or none do (all-or-nothing). Consistency: a transaction moves the DB from one valid state to another, respecting constraints. Isolation: concurrent transactions don't see each other's half-finished work. Durability: once committed, data survives a crash (written to disk/WAL).
topics.example:
A: -100 ──┐
          ├── one transaction: both apply or both roll back
B: +100 ──┘

BEGIN;
  UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 100 WHERE id = 1;  -- debit A
  UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 100 WHERE id = 2;  -- credit B
COMMIT;  -- atomic: crash between the two = full rollback

Real world: server dies after the debit but before the credit: on restart the DB replays the WAL and rolls the half-done transaction back, money never vanishes. Durability = the WAL is fsynced to disk before COMMIT returns. Checkout flows wrap order row + payment row + stock decrement in one transaction for the same reason.

a: Isolation level = how much one transaction is allowed to 'see' of another's uncommitted or concurrent changes. Stricter = safer but slower.

Read Uncommitted: can see uncommitted changes (dirty reads). Read Committed (Postgres default): only sees committed data, but a re-read within the same transaction can change (non-repeatable read). Repeatable Read: rows you read stay stable for the whole transaction, but new matching rows can appear (phantom read). Serializable: transactions behave as if run one after another. No anomalies, but the most locking and retries.
Phenomena to name-drop: dirty read, non-repeatable read, phantom read, lost update.
topics.example:
level            │ dirty │ non-repeat │ phantom
read uncommitted │  yes  │    yes     │  yes
read committed   │  no   │    yes     │  yes   ← Postgres default
repeatable read  │  no   │    no      │  yes
serializable     │  no   │    no      │  no

BEGIN ISOLATION LEVEL REPEATABLE READ;
SELECT balance FROM accounts WHERE id = 1;  -- same answer for whole transaction

Real world: normal CRUD runs fine on Read Committed. Long reports use Repeatable Read for a stable snapshot (numbers don't shift mid-report). Money movement uses Serializable plus a retry loop: Postgres aborts one transaction with a serialization error instead of allowing an anomaly.

a: An index is a separate data structure (usually a B-Tree) that lets the DB find rows without scanning the whole table. It trades write speed and storage for read speed.

B-Tree index: default, good for equality and range queries (=, <, >, BETWEEN, ORDER BY). Hash index: fast equality lookups only. Composite (multi-column) index: order matters. It helps queries that filter on a left-to-right prefix of the columns. Covering index: includes every column a query needs so it never touches the table (index-only scan).
Cost: every INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE must update every index on that table too. Don't over-index write-heavy tables.
topics.example:
Seq scan:  row1 ▶ row2 ▶ ... ▶ row 10,000,000   (reads everything)
B-Tree:    root ▶ branch ▶ leaf ▶ row pointer     (3-4 hops, even at 10M rows)

CREATE INDEX idx_orders_user_created ON orders(user_id, created_at);
-- helps: WHERE user_id = 5 AND created_at > '2026-01-01'
-- helps: WHERE user_id = 5             (leftmost prefix)
-- useless: WHERE created_at > '2026-01-01'   (skips the first column)

Real world: EXPLAIN showing Seq Scan on a big table is the classic slow-query smell, add the index and it flips to Index Scan. A write-heavy events table with 8 indexes updates 8 trees per insert: inserts crawl. Postgres primary keys get a B-Tree index automatically.

a: Use EXPLAIN / EXPLAIN ANALYZE to see the query planner's chosen path (seq scan vs index scan, join order, estimated vs actual rows) before guessing.

Common wins: add an index on filter/join/order-by columns, avoid SELECT *, avoid functions on indexed columns in WHERE (kills index usage), fix N+1 queries (one query per loop iteration) with JOIN or eager loading and watch for implicit type casts that force a full scan.
topics.example:
N+1: 50 orders ▶ loop ▶ 50 user queries = 51 round trips
Fix: SELECT * FROM orders o JOIN users u ON u.id = o.user_id  (1 query)

EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT * FROM orders WHERE user_id = 5;
  Seq Scan on orders  (actual rows=2400000)   -- before: reads whole table
  Index Scan using idx_user  (actual rows=120) -- after CREATE INDEX

Real world: WHERE DATE(created_at) = '2026-08-15' kills the index (function on column), rewrite as a range: created_at >= '2026-08-15' AND created_at < '2026-08-16'. ORMs cause most N+1s silently: Django select_related, Rails includes, GORM Preload fix them.

a: Caching stores hot data in memory to skip expensive DB or computation round trips. Redis: rich data structures (strings, hashes, lists, sets, sorted sets), persistence options, pub/sub, TTLs. Closer to an in-memory data store. Memcached: pure key-value, multi-threaded, simpler and slightly faster for plain get/set at scale, no persistence.

Patterns: cache-aside (app checks cache, falls back to DB, then fills cache: most common), write-through (write cache and DB together), write-behind (write cache, flush to DB async). Always set a TTL and have an invalidation plan. Cache invalidation is famously one of the two hard problems in CS.
topics.example:
Cache-aside:
 app ─▶ Redis GET user:42 ── hit: return (~1ms)
              │ miss
              └▶ Postgres SELECT (~30ms) ─▶ SETEX user:42 300 ─▶ return

Python:
  val = r.get(key)                     # try cache first
  if not val:
      val = db.fetch(key); r.setex(key, 300, val)   # fill with 5 min TTL

Real world: session store and rate-limit counters live in Redis, not Postgres. A 30ms profile query behind a 1ms cache cuts DB load ~97% at high traffic. Forgot TTL = stale data forever after the row changes: the invalidation plan matters more than the caching.

a: SQL (Postgres/MySQL): fixed schema, strong ACID transactions, relational joins. Best when data is structured and consistency matters (money, inventory).

NoSQL isn't one thing: document stores (MongoDB: flexible JSON-like docs), key-value (DynamoDB, Redis: simple, extremely fast), wide-column (Cassandra: huge write volume, time-series), graph (Neo4j: relationships-first). Trade-offs usually follow CAP: many NoSQL stores favor availability and partition tolerance over strict consistency, settling for eventual consistency.
topics.example:
One e-commerce app, four stores:
 orders, payments    ─▶ Postgres   (ACID, joins)
 product catalog     ─▶ MongoDB    (every category has different fields)
 sessions, counters  ─▶ Redis      (speed + TTL)
 clickstream events  ─▶ Cassandra  (massive append-only writes)

Real world: banks stay on SQL because a lost update is real money. DynamoDB gives single-digit ms reads at any scale but no joins: you model around access patterns instead. Most products start Postgres-only and add NoSQL pieces when one workload outgrows it.

a: Locking controls concurrent access to the same row or table. Pessimistic locking: lock the row up front (SELECT ... FOR UPDATE) and block others until commit. Safe but cuts concurrency. Optimistic locking: don't lock. Check a version column at write time and reject if it changed. Better throughput, needs a retry loop.
Deadlock: two transactions each hold a lock the other needs. The DB detects it and kills one (deadlock victim). Avoid by always acquiring locks in the same order.
topics.example:
Pessimistic: T2 waits at the lock ░░░░ until T1 commits
Optimistic:  both proceed, loser fails the version check ─▶ reload, retry

SELECT * FROM seats WHERE id = 7 FOR UPDATE;   -- pessimistic: row locked

UPDATE accounts SET balance = 90, version = 6
WHERE id = 1 AND version = 5;   -- optimistic: 0 rows = someone won, retry

Real world: seat and ticket booking uses FOR UPDATE: two buyers must not hold the same seat. ORMs ship optimistic locking as a version column (JPA @Version, Django F() updates). Hot counters skip both: a single atomic UPDATE counter = counter + 1 needs no explicit lock.

a: Replication: copy the same data to multiple nodes for availability and read scaling. Primary-replica (leader-follower): writes go to the primary, reads can go to replicas (mind the replication lag). Multi-leader and leaderless setups exist but add conflict resolution complexity.
Sharding (partitioning): split a huge table across nodes by a shard key (user_id range or hash) so no single node holds everything. Scales writes, but cross-shard joins and transactions get hard.
topics.example:
Replication (same data, copies)     Sharding (split data)
 primary ──▶ replica 1 (reads)        users 0-4M  ─▶ shard A
         └─▶ replica 2 (reads)        users 4-8M  ─▶ shard B
 writes hit primary only              key: hash(user_id) % shards

Real world: replication lag bites as read-your-writes: user saves profile, next page reads a stale replica, edit looks lost. Fix: read own writes from the primary briefly. Instagram sharded Postgres by user id: all one user's data on one shard keeps queries single-shard. Combine both: each shard has its own replicas.

a: Postgres MVCC: an UPDATE never overwrites a row, it writes a new row version; each version carries xmin/xmax (creating/deleting transaction IDs) and every transaction sees only versions visible to its snapshot. Readers never block writers and writers never block readers.

Cost: old versions become dead tuples (bloat). VACUUM reclaims them; autovacuum does it in the background. If autovacuum falls behind on a hot table, the table and its indexes bloat and scans slow down. Also prevents transaction ID wraparound, which is why you never disable it.
Interview line: long-running transactions are dangerous in Postgres because VACUUM cannot clean anything their snapshot might still see.
topics.example:
UPDATE writes a new version, never overwrites:
 row v1 (xmin=100, xmax=205) ← old version stays for old snapshots
 row v2 (xmin=205)           ← new version appended
 VACUUM removes v1 once no snapshot can still see it

SELECT relname, n_dead_tup FROM pg_stat_user_tables;  -- bloat check
VACUUM (ANALYZE, VERBOSE) orders;  -- reclaim dead tuples by hand

Real world: a batch job holds one transaction open for 2 hours while orders takes heavy updates. VACUUM must keep every version that snapshot might see, dead tuples pile up, the table bloats 3x, p99 climbs. Fix: chunk the batch into short transactions. Autovacuum also prevents transaction ID wraparound: the failure mode that turns a whole DB read-only.

a: Write-Ahead Log: every change is appended to the WAL and fsynced before it is considered committed; data pages in memory are flushed later at checkpoints. Crash recovery replays WAL from the last checkpoint. This is the D in ACID.

The WAL is also the replication stream: streaming replication ships WAL to replicas (async by default: small lag window; synchronous: zero loss but slower commits). Logical replication/CDC (Debezium) decodes WAL into row-change events, which is how you feed Kafka from Postgres without dual writes.
topics.example:
write ─▶ WAL append + fsync ─▶ COMMIT returns
            │ later, in batches
            └▶ checkpoint flushes data pages to disk
crash ─▶ replay WAL since last checkpoint: nothing committed is lost

The same WAL feeds replicas:
 streaming (async): replica seconds behind, fast commits
 streaming (sync):  commit waits for the replica, zero loss
 logical / CDC:     Debezium decodes WAL ─▶ Kafka row events

Real world: payments run synchronous_commit = on with a sync replica: RPO zero. Analytics replicas stay async: seconds of lag is fine there. CDC from the WAL is how you feed Kafka from Postgres without dual writes.

a: Each Postgres connection is a whole OS process with real memory cost, so max_connections is small (low hundreds). Kubernetes makes this a trap: 50 pods × 20 connections in each app pool = 1000 connections and Postgres falls over.

PgBouncer sits in front and multiplexes thousands of client connections onto few real ones. Modes: session (1 client = 1 server conn while connected, safest), transaction (server conn borrowed per transaction, the usual choice, but session state like prepared statements and SET breaks), statement (rarely used).
App side: always use a pool with a max, sane idle timeout and a connect timeout, so a slow DB causes fast failures instead of goroutine/thread pileups.
topics.example:
No pooler:  50 pods × 20 conns = 1000 ─▶ Postgres (max_connections 100) ✗
PgBouncer:  50 pods ─▶ pooler ─▶ ~80 real connections ✓

pgbouncer.ini:
  pool_mode = transaction   # server conn borrowed per transaction

Go:
  db.SetMaxOpenConns(5)   // per-pod cap: fail fast, no pileup

Real world: a deploy doubles pod count, the DB hits max_connections, everything errors. Fix: PgBouncer in transaction mode plus app pools capped at 5 per pod, ~80 real connections total. Same hardware, no more connection storms. The ceiling is low because every Postgres connection is a full OS process.

a: GIN: inverted index for multi-value columns: jsonb containment (@>), arrays, full-text search. Slower to update, great to query. GiST: geometric/nearest-neighbor searches, powers PostGIS: directly relevant to delivery radius and rider proximity queries. BRIN: tiny index storing min/max per block range, perfect for huge append-only tables queried by time.

Partial index: index only rows matching a WHERE clause: small and fast when queries always target a subset (active orders). Expression index: index a computed value like lower(email) so the query can use it.
topics.example:
GIN        ─ jsonb @>, arrays, full-text (inverted index)
GiST       ─ geo + nearest-neighbor, powers PostGIS
BRIN       ─ min/max per block: huge append-only time-series
Partial    ─ only rows matching a WHERE
Expression ─ index a computed value like lower(email)

CREATE INDEX ON orders (restaurant_id)
  WHERE status IN ('placed', 'preparing');  -- live orders only

Real world: the partial index holds thousands of live orders instead of millions of all-time ones, so dispatch queries stay fast and delivered orders fall out automatically. Rider-proximity search runs on a GiST index via PostGIS. BRIN on an append-only events table is megabytes where a B-Tree would be gigabytes.

a: Persistence: RDB = periodic snapshots (compact, fast restart, can lose minutes on crash). AOF = append every write (configurable fsync, minimal loss, bigger files, slower restart). Common production setup: both, or RDB only when Redis is a pure cache and loss is fine.

Eviction at maxmemory: noeviction (writes error: default, wrong for caches), allkeys-lru (evict least-recently-used anywhere: the usual cache choice), volatile-lru (only keys with TTL), allkeys-lfu (frequency-based). Wrong policy is a classic prod incident: cache fills, writes start failing.
One more: Redis is single-threaded for commands, so one slow command (KEYS *, huge SMEMBERS) blocks everything. Use SCAN, keep values small.
topics.example:
RDB: snapshot every N minutes ── compact, fast restart, can lose minutes
AOF: append every write       ── minimal loss, bigger file, slower restart
maxmemory reached ─▶ eviction policy decides what dies

redis-cli:
  CONFIG SET maxmemory-policy allkeys-lru   # the usual cache choice
  INFO stats                                # watch evicted_keys + hit rate

Real world: a cache cluster hits maxmemory with noeviction: SETs start erroring, hit rate collapses, the DB takes the full read load and browns out. Fix: allkeys-lru plus alerts on evicted_keys. And one slow KEYS * blocks the whole single-threaded server: use SCAN instead.

topics.q: Cache Stampede, Hot Keys & Distributed Locks
a: Stampede (thundering herd): a popular key expires and 5,000 concurrent requests all miss and hit the DB at once. Fixes: per-key mutex so one request recomputes while the rest wait or serve stale, TTL jitter so keys don't expire together, background refresh before expiry for known-hot keys.

Hot key: one key (top restaurant's menu) takes so much traffic that its Redis shard saturates. Fixes: replicate the value under N suffixed keys and read a random one, or add a small in-process cache with a short TTL in front.

Distributed lock: SET key value NX PX 30000, delete only if value matches (Lua) so you never release someone else's lock. Redlock exists but is debated; for correctness-critical exclusion prefer DB row locks or a consensus store and say that in the interview.
topics.example:
Stampede: hot key expires ─▶ 5000 requests miss ─▶ 5000 DB queries
Fix:      1 request recomputes ██, 4999 serve stale ░░ for 2s

Redis lock (one recomputer wins):
  SET lock:menu42 token NX PX 30000   # only the first caller gets it

Go:
  g.Do("menu42", fetchMenu)   // singleflight: dedupes concurrent calls

Real world: iftar spike: menu:top-restaurant expires at peak and the DB gets hammered. Fix: per-key singleflight (one recompute, the rest serve stale), TTL 300s plus random 30s jitter so keys never expire together, a background worker refreshes the top-100 menus every 60s. Hot key trick: copy the value under N suffixed keys and read a random one.

a: Encapsulation: bundle data with the methods that operate on it and hide internal state behind a small public surface (private fields, expose only what callers need). Abstraction: expose what a thing does, hide how (interfaces, abstract types). Inheritance: an is-a relationship reusing a parent's behavior; powerful but the tightest coupling in OOP. Polymorphism: one interface, many implementations; the caller invokes the method without knowing which concrete type answers.
Interview trap: encapsulation vs abstraction sound alike. Encapsulation hides state (implementation data), abstraction hides complexity (implementation logic).
topics.example:
PaymentMethod (interface): pay(amount)
 ├── CreditCard.pay()
 ├── ApplePay.pay()
 └── CashOnDelivery.pay()   ← checkout never branches on the type

Python:
  class PaymentMethod(Protocol):
      def pay(self, amount): ...        # abstraction: what, not how
  def checkout(m): m.pay(total)         # polymorphism kills the if/else chain

Go:
  type PaymentMethod interface { Pay(amount int) error }
  func Checkout(m PaymentMethod) { m.Pay(total) }   // any implementation fits

Real world: Stripe's SDK charges cards, wallets and bank debits through one call shape. Encapsulation in practice: an Account exposes deposit() and hides its balance field so nothing writes it directly. Every ORM model is abstraction: you call save(), never see the SQL.

a: Inheritance: is-a. The subclass is tightly coupled to parent internals and deep hierarchies turn fragile: change a base class and every child can break (the fragile base class problem). Composition: has-a. Build behavior by combining small objects; parts are swappable at runtime and testable in isolation.

The answer interviewers want: prefer composition, reach for inheritance only on a genuine, stable is-a relationship. Go dropped inheritance entirely in favor of embedding and even classic Java guidance says favor composition.
topics.example:
Bad (is-a tree):  Vehicle ◀── Car ◀── ElectricCar   (hybrid breaks the tree)
Good (has-a):     Car { engine }, engine = Electric | Petrol | Hybrid

Python:
  class Car:
      def __init__(self, engine): self.engine = engine   # part injected, swappable

Go:
  type Car struct { engine Engine }   // interface field: any engine fits
  // Go has no inheritance: only embedding + interfaces

Real world: Go's standard library composes tiny interfaces (io.Reader, io.Writer) instead of class trees. React docs say use composition, not component inheritance. Game engines moved from deep class hierarchies to entity-component systems for the same reason.

a: Interface: a pure contract, no state, a class can implement many. Use for capabilities shared across unrelated types (Comparable, PaymentGateway, Notifiable). Abstract class: can hold state and partial implementation, single inheritance only. Use to share a code skeleton among closely related subclasses (template method pattern).

Modern languages blur the line (Java default methods, Kotlin interfaces with bodies), but the decision rule survives: contract across unrelated types → interface; shared skeleton within one family → abstract class.

S (Single Responsibility): a class or module has one reason to change. O (Open/Closed): open for extension, closed for modification. Add behavior with new code, not by editing tested code. L (Liskov Substitution): a subclass must work anywhere its parent is expected without breaking correctness. I (Interface Segregation): several small focused interfaces beat one fat one that clients must depend on fully. D (Dependency Inversion): depend on abstractions, not concrete implementations. High-level modules shouldn't depend on low-level details.
topics.example:
D in one picture:
 OrderService ──▶ PaymentGateway (interface) ◀── StripeGateway
  high level depends on the abstraction; the concrete class plugs in

Python:
  class OrderService:
      def __init__(self, gateway): self.gateway = gateway   # inject the abstraction

Go:
  type PaymentGateway interface { Charge(cents int) error }
  func NewOrderService(g PaymentGateway) *OrderService      // fake in tests, Stripe in prod

Real world: adding a new shipping method as a new class with zero edits to checkout = Open/Closed. Square extending Rectangle and breaking setWidth is the classic Liskov violation. A fat interface forcing a printer class to implement fax() = Interface Segregation smell.

a: Singleton: exactly one instance app-wide (a DB connection pool). Use sparingly: it is global state. Factory: centralizes object creation so callers never name concrete classes. Strategy: interchangeable algorithms behind one interface, swappable at runtime. Observer: subscribers get notified when a subject's state changes (in-process pub/sub). Repository: data access behind an interface so business logic doesn't depend on the specific ORM or DB.
topics.example:
Strategy:
 ShippingCost (interface) ◀── Standard | Express | Free
 checkout picks one at runtime: no if/else chain spread through the code

Python:
  order.shipping = ExpressShipping()    # swap behavior at runtime
  cost = order.shipping.cost(order)

Go:
  var s Shipping = FreeShipping{}   // same call site, different behavior
  total += s.Cost(order)

Real world: every UI event listener is Observer. Go's database/sql is Factory plus Repository flavored: one interface, many drivers registered by name. Most logging libraries ship a singleton default logger. Strategy shows up in pricing, shipping, tax and retry policies.

a: Instead of a class building its own dependencies (tight coupling), dependencies come from outside: constructor, setter or a DI container. Tests get easy (swap in fakes) and wiring changes without editing the class itself.
topics.example:
Without DI: OrderService ──creates──▶ StripeGateway   (hard-wired, untestable)
With DI:    OrderService(gateway)   ◀── prod: Stripe, tests: fake

Python:
  class OrderService:
      def __init__(self, gateway): self.gateway = gateway   # injected
  OrderService(FakeGateway())      # unit test: no network call

Go:
  func NewOrderService(g PaymentGateway) *OrderService   // constructor injection

Real world: Spring and NestJS are DI containers: they build the whole object graph. Go culture skips the framework and wires by hand in main(). Every mock in your unit tests exists because of this pattern.

a: Organize code into layers with a strict dependency direction: presentation (controllers/API) → application (use cases/services) → domain (core entities and rules) → infrastructure (DB, external APIs). Core idea from Clean and Hexagonal architecture: business logic must not depend on frameworks, databases or UI. Those are details that plug into the core through interfaces, not the other way around. So you can swap infrastructure (Postgres → DynamoDB) without touching business rules.

Ubiquitous language: the team and the code use the exact same domain terms, so methods read the way the business talks. A bounded context is the boundary inside which one model and one language stay consistent: the same word can mean different things in different contexts and that is fine as long as the boundary is explicit.

Bounded contexts are the best starting point for microservice boundaries: roughly one context per service. Context mapping describes the relationships between them; an anti-corruption layer translates another context's model at the border so it never leaks into yours.
topics.example:
Checkout context               Logistics context
 'Order' = cart, payment,       'Order' = pickup point, rider, ETA
           promo codes
      └── OrderPlaced event ──▶ ACL translates ──▶ Delivery model

Go:
  func FromOrderPlaced(e OrderPlaced) Delivery   // anti-corruption layer: their model stops at the border

Real world: 'customer' means payer in billing but ticket owner in support: two contexts, two models, both correct. A food delivery app splits checkout service and logistics service on exactly this line: logistics consumes OrderPlaced and builds its own Delivery. Naming code with the business words (ubiquitous language) kills translation bugs between requirements and code.

a: Entity: has an identity that persists over time (User #42 stays the same user as fields change). Value object: no identity, immutable, compared by value (Money(10, 'SAR'), an Address). Prefer value objects where possible: immutable things are safer to reason about.

Aggregate: a cluster of entities and value objects treated as one consistency unit, with a single aggregate root that outside code must go through. Invariants (order total equals sum of lines) are enforced by the root. Rule: one transaction updates one aggregate; effects on other aggregates go through domain events, eventually consistent.
topics.example:
Order  (aggregate root, entity: has identity)
 ├── OrderLine ×3        (child entities, only the root touches them)
 ├── Money(120, 'SAR')   (value object: immutable, compared by value)
 └── Address             (value object)

Go:
  type Money struct { Amount int; Currency string }   // value object
  func (o *Order) AddItem(p Product, qty int) error   // root enforces invariants

Real world: outside code never sets line.qty directly. It calls order.AddItem(product, qty) and the root revalidates (max items, total = sum of lines). The repository loads and saves the whole Order as one unit. Two Money(10, 'SAR') values are equal, but two users with the same name are still different users: value vs identity.

a: Repository: one per aggregate root, gives the domain collection-like access (FindByID, Save) and hides the database. Domain event: a fact that happened, named in past tense (OrderPlaced), used to trigger reactions in other aggregates or contexts without direct coupling.

Outbox pattern: saving the aggregate and publishing the event must not half-fail. Write the event into an outbox table in the same DB transaction as the aggregate, then a relay publishes it to Kafka/PubSub and marks it sent. Guarantees at-least-once publishing; consumers stay idempotent.
topics.example:
One DB transaction:
 ┌ INSERT INTO orders ...             ┐
 └ INSERT INTO outbox (OrderPlaced)   ┘  atomic: both rows or neither
      relay polls outbox ─▶ publishes to Kafka ─▶ marks row sent

Go:
  tx.Exec(insertOrder)
  tx.Exec(insertOutboxEvent)   // same tx as the order: cannot half-fail
  tx.Commit()

Real world: crash right after commit: the event sits in outbox and the next poll publishes it, nothing lost. Debezium implements the relay by tailing the table. Publishing is at-least-once, so consumers dedupe by event id (idempotent handlers). Without outbox: order saved, Kafka publish fails, logistics never hears about the order.

topics.q: Test Pyramid (Unit vs Integration vs E2E)
a: Unit tests: fast, isolated, test one function/class with dependencies faked. The base of the pyramid, you want the most of these. Integration tests: verify real pieces working together (your code plus a real Postgres/Redis/broker). Fewer and slower. E2E tests: drive the whole deployed system through its public API or UI. Fewest, slowest, most brittle.
Anti-pattern: the ice-cream cone (mostly e2e, few unit tests). The suite gets slow and flaky and the feedback loop dies.
topics.example:
/   e2e   \      ~5    whole system, slowest, most brittle
     / integration\    ~30   real Postgres/Redis in Docker
    /     unit     \   ~200  pure logic, milliseconds

Python:
  def test_discount(): assert price(100, 'SAVE10') == 90   # unit: no DB, no network

Go:
  cases := []struct{ in, want int }{{100, 90}, {50, 45}}   // table-driven unit test

Real world: CI ladder: unit tests on every push (seconds), integration tests per PR against containers (minutes), 5 e2e happy paths on staging before deploy. Ice-cream cone teams (mostly e2e) wait 40 minutes to learn a typo broke checkout.

a: Test double = any stand-in for a real dependency. Stub: returns canned answers, no assertions. Mock: also verifies interactions (was sendEmail called exactly once with X). Fake: a real but lightweight implementation, like an in-memory repository. Spy: records calls for later inspection.

Rule of thumb: test behavior, not implementation. Over-mocking couples tests to internals, so refactors break tests even when behavior is unchanged. Prefer fakes for interfaces you own, mock only at true external boundaries (payment gateway, email).
topics.example:
stub: returns canned answers        (no checks)
fake: working mini implementation   (in-memory repo)
mock: verifies the interaction      (charge called once?)
spy:  records calls for later inspection

Python:
  repo = FakeOrderRepo()                    # fake: real behavior, in memory
  gateway.charge.assert_called_once()       # mock: verify the interaction

Go:
  type FakeRepo struct{ m map[int]Order }   // fake: implements the interface

Real world: OrderService test injects a fake repo plus a mocked payment gateway: asserts order saved as paid and charge called exactly once, runs in milliseconds. Over-mocked suites break on every refactor even when behavior is unchanged. Mock only true externals (Stripe, email), fake what you own.

a: Testcontainers pattern: spin up a real Postgres/Kafka/Redis in Docker for integration tests, so tests hit the same engine as production instead of an in-memory imitation.

Consumer-driven contract testing (Pact): the consumer publishes a contract describing exactly what it calls and what shape it expects back; the provider's CI replays that contract against the real service. Catches breaking API changes without a shared staging environment or a slow e2e suite.
topics.example:
consumer (checkout) ── contract: GET /menu-items/42 ▶ {id, price, available}
                            │ published to a contract broker
provider (menu) CI ──▶ replays contract against real service
                       rename price ▶ unit_price = provider build fails

Python:
  postgres = PostgresContainer('postgres:16')   # testcontainers: real engine in Docker

Go:
  pgc, _ := tcpostgres.Run(ctx, "postgres:16")   // same idea, Go testcontainers

Real world: checkout-service publishes what it expects from menu-service (Pact). menu-service CI verifies every build against that contract, so a breaking rename fails at build time, not in production. Testcontainers replaced in-memory DB fakes because SQLite-in-tests hid Postgres-only bugs.

a: TDD loop: red (write a failing test first), green (simplest code that passes), refactor (clean up with the test as a safety net). Even without strict TDD the mindset matters: every bug fix starts with a failing test that reproduces the bug, so it can never silently return.
Deterministic tests: no sleeps, no real clocks, no shared mutable state between tests. Inject time and randomness so you control them. Flaky tests destroy trust in the whole suite.
topics.example:
red ──▶ green ──▶ refactor ──▶ red ...
 │ failing     │ simplest      │ clean up,
 │ test first  │ code to pass  │ tests as safety net

Python:
  def test_retry_applies_one_discount():   # red: reproduces the bug first
      assert retried_order.total == 90

Go:
  t.Run("retry applies one discount", ...)   // bug fix starts as a failing test

Real world: bug: discount applied twice on retry. Write the failing test, fix with an idempotency check, the test stays forever as a regression guard. Flaky suite fix: replace time.sleep waits with an injected fake clock, tests get deterministic and fast.

a: Authentication (AuthN): verifying who you are (login: password, OTP, biometric, SSO). Authorization (AuthZ): verifying what you may do once identified (permissions, roles, scopes). Often confused but separate steps. You can be authenticated yet not authorized for a specific action.
topics.example:
request ─▶ AuthN: who is this?    (bad login ─▶ 401 Unauthorized)
        └▶ AuthZ: may they do it? (no permission ─▶ 403 Forbidden)

Python:
  user = verify_token(request)         # AuthN: identity, 401 if invalid
  if not user.is_admin: abort(403)     # AuthZ: permission check

Go:
  user, err := auth.Verify(token)              // AuthN: who
  if !user.Can("orders:delete") { deny(403) }  // AuthZ: what

Real world: you log in fine (authenticated), then delete another user's account and get 403 (not authorized). Status codes tell the story: 401 means 'who are you', 403 means 'I know you, still no'. Company admin panel: everyone logs in through the same door, roles decide who sees what.

a: A regularly updated list of the most critical web app security risks, maintained by OWASP. Useful shorthand vocabulary in interviews. Recurring themes: broken access control (missing authorization checks), cryptographic failures (weak or missing encryption), injection (SQL, command), insecure design, security misconfiguration, vulnerable or outdated components, identification and authentication failures, software and data integrity failures, logging and monitoring failures, plus server-side request forgery (SSRF).
topics.example:
GET /api/orders/123
  check 1: logged in?  yes ─▶ return order 123
  missing: does order 123 belong to THIS user?   ← IDOR

The missing line:
  order = db.get(order_id)
  if order.user_id != current_user.id: abort(403)   # ownership check

Real world: broken access control sits at #1 on the list and IDOR is its classic form: change a numeric id in the URL, see someone else's data. Bug bounty programs at Meta and Shopify pay out for exactly this constantly. Log4Shell (2021) made 'vulnerable components' concrete: one logging library, internet on fire.

a: SQL injection happens when untrusted user input is concatenated straight into a SQL query, letting an attacker change the query's meaning. Prevention: parameterized queries / prepared statements (the driver keeps input strictly as data, never executable SQL) or an ORM that does this by default. Never manual string escaping.
topics.example:
Query:   SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = '<input>'
Input:   ' OR '1'='1
Becomes: WHERE email = '' OR '1'='1'   ← always true, returns every row

Python:
  cur.execute(f"... WHERE email = '{email}'")     # vulnerable: input becomes SQL
  cur.execute("... WHERE email = %s", (email,))   # safe: input stays data

Go:
  db.Query("SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = $1", email)  // placeholder, safe

Real world: the xkcd 'Bobby Tables' comic is this exact bug. The 2015 TalkTalk breach started as SQLi in one web form. Every mainstream ORM parameterizes by default, so raw string-built SQL is the code review red flag.

a: XSS (Cross-Site Scripting): attacker injects malicious JavaScript into a page other users view. It runs in the victim's browser with their session and can steal cookies or tokens. Prevention: escape or sanitize any user content rendered as HTML, set a Content-Security-Policy and mark cookies HttpOnly.

CSRF (Cross-Site Request Forgery): tricks a logged-in user's browser into sending an unwanted request to a site they are authenticated on, because browsers auto-attach cookies. Prevention: CSRF tokens, SameSite cookies and origin checks.
topics.example:
XSS:  attacker's script in a comment ─▶ victim's browser runs it as the site
CSRF: attacker's page ─▶ hidden form ─▶ bank.com (browser attaches your cookie)

Memory hook: XSS = attacker's code runs ON the site. CSRF = attacker uses YOUR logged-in browser FROM another site.

Defenses:
  html.escape(user_comment)                        # XSS: render as text, not HTML
  Set-Cookie: session=x; SameSite=Lax; HttpOnly    # CSRF + cookie theft

Real world: the MySpace Samy worm (2005) was XSS: one profile infected a million users in a day. React JSX and Django templates escape by default, danger comes back with dangerouslySetInnerHTML or the safe filter. Chrome defaulting cookies to SameSite=Lax killed most classic CSRF.

a: Session-based: server creates a session on login, stores it server-side (Redis, DB) and gives the client a session ID cookie. The server can revoke instantly, but scaling needs shared session storage across instances. JWT (JSON Web Token): a signed self-contained token holding claims (user id, roles, expiry). Any server verifies the signature without a DB lookup: stateless, easy to scale. But revoking one JWT before it expires is hard (needs a blocklist, which reintroduces state).
topics.example:
Session: cookie sid=abc ─▶ server looks up abc in Redis ─▶ identity (revoke anytime)
JWT:     header.payload.signature ─▶ verify signature locally ─▶ trust the claims

JWT shape: eyJhbGci... . eyJzdWIiOiI0MiJ9 . x7Kp...
           base64, readable by anyone! signed, not encrypted

Python:
  jwt.decode(token, key, algorithms=["HS256"])   # verify + read claims, no DB hit

Real world: microservices verify JWTs locally, no auth-service call per request. Standard combo: 15 min access token + refresh token, so a leaked token has a small damage window. The 'log out everywhere' button is the session model's win: delete the server rows. JWT needs a blocklist hack for that.

a: OAuth2 is an authorization framework: a user grants a third-party app limited access to their data on another service without sharing their password. The core output is an access token. OpenID Connect (OIDC) sits on top of OAuth2 for authentication: it adds an ID token (a JWT) proving who the user is, standardizing login.

Common flow: Authorization Code flow (with PKCE for mobile and SPA clients). App redirects to the provider, user approves, provider redirects back with a code, the app exchanges the code server-side for tokens.
topics.example:
app ─▶ redirect to Google (scope: openid calendar)
user ─▶ approves on Google's page (password never touches the app)
Google ─▶ redirect back with one-time code
app server ─▶ exchange code ─▶ ID token (who) + access token (what)

Memory hook: OAuth2 = what the app may access. OIDC = who the user is.

Real world: 'Sign in with Google/GitHub' is OIDC. A scheduling app reading your Google Calendar uses the OAuth2 access token with the calendar scope only. PKCE became mandatory for mobile because the redirect back to the app can be intercepted without it.

a: Encryption: reversible with the right key, protects confidentiality. Symmetric (one key both ways, fast: AES) vs asymmetric (public key encrypts, private key decrypts: RSA/ECC, slower, used for key exchange and signatures). Hashing: one-way, deterministic, fixed-size output. Used for passwords and integrity checks. A good password hash (bcrypt, argon2) is deliberately slow to resist brute force. Encoding (Base64, URL-encoding): not security at all. Just a reversible format change anyone can undo.
topics.example:
encryption: data + key ─▶ ciphertext ── key ──▶ data again (two-way, secret)
hashing:    data ─▶ digest                         (one-way, no way back)
encoding:   data ─▶ base64 ─▶ data again           (two-way, no secret at all)

Python:
  bcrypt.hashpw(pw, bcrypt.gensalt())   # slow on purpose, per-user salt
  base64.b64encode(data)                # NOT security, anyone decodes

Real world: passwords get hashed (bcrypt/argon2), never encrypted: nobody should recover them, only verify a match. Card numbers you must show later get AES encryption with keys in a KMS. Interview trap: 'we base64 our tokens for security' is wrong by definition.

a: Beyond the handshake: TLS certificates are issued by a Certificate Authority (CA) and chain up to a root CA the browser trusts. The HSTS header (HTTP Strict Transport Security) makes browsers always use HTTPS for a domain, killing downgrade attacks. Certificate pinning (mostly mobile apps) hard-codes the expected certificate or key to resist even a compromised CA.
topics.example:
trust chain: bank.com cert ─▶ intermediate CA ─▶ root CA (in browser trust store)

Header:
  Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=63072000; includeSubDomains
  # browser: never try plain HTTP on this domain for 2 years

Real world: HSTS closes the first-visit gap where a man-in-the-middle could catch the one plain HTTP request before the HTTPS redirect. Let's Encrypt automated free certificates and pushed the web past 90% HTTPS. Mobile banking apps pin their certificate so even a cert from a rogue CA fails.

a: Monolith: one deployable app, one codebase. Simple to develop and deploy early, but scaling and team ownership get harder as it grows.

Microservices: the app splits into small independently deployable services (each owns its own data), talking over the network (REST/gRPC/events). Gains: independent scaling, deploys and team ownership. Costs: network latency, distributed debugging, data consistency across services and more moving parts to monitor and deploy.
topics.example:
Monolith                      Microservices
 ┌────────────┐                orders ────▶ own DB
 │ orders     │                payments ──▶ own DB
 │ payments   │  one DB        inventory ─▶ own DB
 │ inventory  │  one deploy    talk via REST + Kafka events
 └────────────┘

Real world: Shopify runs a famous modular monolith at huge scale: monolith is not a junior choice. Netflix and Amazon split into services when team count, not traffic, forced it: deploys blocked each other. Rule of thumb: start with a monolith, split when teams step on each other, not before.

a: Docker packages an app + its dependencies into an image, run as an isolated container sharing the host OS kernel (lighter than a VM). An image is built in layers (each Dockerfile instruction = a cached layer), which makes rebuilds fast when only the top layers change.

Key objects: Image (the blueprint), Container (a running instance of an image), Dockerfile (build recipe), Volume (persistent storage outside the container's writable layer), Registry (Docker Hub, ECR: stores images).
topics.example:
Image (layered recipe) ── docker run ──▶ Container (running instance)
 layer 3: COPY . .          ← changes often, rebuilt each time
 layer 2: RUN npm ci        ← cached while package.json is unchanged
 layer 1: FROM node:20-slim

FROM node:20-slim
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci --only=production   # cached layer: skipped on rebuild
COPY . .
CMD ["node", "server.js"]

Real world: a VM boots a whole OS, a container starts a process in milliseconds sharing the host kernel. Copying package.json before the source keeps the npm install layer cached: CI builds drop from minutes to seconds. Registries (Docker Hub, ECR) store tagged images the way git stores commits: push, pull, roll back to any tag.

a: Kubernetes (K8s) orchestrates containers across a cluster of machines: scheduling, scaling, self-healing, networking.

Pod: smallest deployable unit, one or more containers sharing network and storage. Deployment: manages a set of replica Pods, handles rolling updates and self-healing. Service: stable network endpoint (ClusterIP/NodePort/LoadBalancer) that load-balances traffic to matching Pods (Pod IPs are ephemeral). Ingress: HTTP(S) routing into the cluster from outside. ConfigMap/Secret: externalize config and sensitive values from the container image.
topics.example:
Ingress (HTTP routing from outside)
   │
Service (stable IP, load-balances)
   │
Deployment (desired state: 3 replicas)
 ├─ Pod api-1    ├─ Pod api-2    └─ Pod api-3

kubectl apply -f deploy.yaml   # declare desired state
kubectl get pods               # K8s makes reality match it

Real world: kill a Pod and the Deployment sees 2 running vs 3 desired, starts a replacement: self-healing with no human. Pod IPs change constantly, which is exactly why the Service exists. The same image runs in staging and prod because config lives in ConfigMap/Secret, not in the image.

a: Horizontal Pod Autoscaler (HPA): automatically adds or removes Pod replicas based on metrics (CPU, memory or custom metrics like queue depth) to match load.

Resource requests vs limits (set per container): requests = what the scheduler reserves for placement, limits = the hard ceiling before the container is throttled (CPU) or OOM-killed (memory). Skipping limits risks noisy neighbors hogging a node; over-reserving requests wastes cluster capacity.
topics.example:
load rises ▶ avg CPU hits 70% ▶ HPA adds Pods: 3 ─▶ 5 ─▶ 8 (max 10)
load drops ▶ HPA scales back down to min 3

resources:
  requests: { cpu: "250m", memory: "256Mi" }   # scheduler reserves this
  limits:   { cpu: "500m", memory: "512Mi" }   # ceiling: throttle or OOM-kill

Real world: dinner-rush traffic doubles, HPA scales the API from 3 to 8 Pods, back to 3 after midnight. Memory limit too low shows up as random OOMKilled restarts. CPU limit too low shows up as throttling: latency climbs while the CPU graph still looks fine.

a: A service mesh (Istio, Linkerd) adds a network layer of sidecar proxies next to each service to handle cross-cutting concerns without changing app code: mTLS encryption between services, retries/timeouts/circuit breaking, traffic shifting (canary) and fine-grained observability (per-hop latency, error rate).
topics.example:
service A ─▶ [sidecar] ══ mTLS ══ [sidecar] ─▶ service B
                └ retries, timeouts, metrics live here, not in app code

Canary via mesh config (no app redeploy):
  95% ──▶ v1
   5% ──▶ v2   # error rate OK? ramp: 25% ▶ 50% ▶ 100%

Real world: Istio and Linkerd inject an Envoy sidecar into every Pod. One rollout gives mTLS between all services with zero app changes. A canary shift is a config edit: route 5% to v2, watch the dashboards, ramp up or roll back without touching code.

a: CI (Continuous Integration): every push triggers automated build + tests, catching integration bugs early. CD (Continuous Delivery/Deployment): automatically packages and ships that build toward production. Delivery stops at a manual approval gate, Deployment goes straight to prod.
A typical pipeline: lint → unit tests → build image → push to registry → deploy to staging → integration/e2e tests → (approval) → deploy to prod, with a rollback step wired in.
topics.example:
push ▶ lint ▶ tests ▶ build image ▶ staging ▶ e2e ▶ (approval) ▶ prod
        └ fail anywhere: pipeline stops, main stays deployable

GitHub Actions on push to main:
  npm test                                    # CI gate
  docker build -t api:$SHA . && docker push   # one image per commit
  kubectl set image deploy/api api=api:$SHA   # roll out the new tag

Real world: CI catches 'works on my machine' at the pull request, not in prod. Smoke test fails after deploy: the pipeline rolls the Deployment back to the previous image tag automatically. Delivery vs Deployment is one question: is there a human approval gate before prod?

a: IaC defines infrastructure (servers, networks, DBs) in version-controlled config files instead of manual console clicks. Reproducible, reviewable and diffable like application code.

Terraform: declarative and provider-agnostic. Describe the desired end state, it figures out the plan. Ansible: mostly imperative, good for config management and app deploys on top of existing servers. Both support plan-before-apply to preview changes.
topics.example:
console clicks: snowflake servers, no history, no review
IaC: git diff ▶ code review ▶ terraform plan ▶ apply ▶ same result every time

resource "aws_instance" "web" {
  ami           = "ami-123456"
  instance_type = "t3.medium"
}
# terraform plan prints create/change/destroy before touching anything

Real world: a new environment is one terraform apply, identical to prod in minutes. Someone edits infra by hand in the console: the next plan shows the drift. Disaster recovery: region down, run the same code against another region.

a: Rolling update: replace old instances with new ones gradually, keeping the service up the whole time (K8s Deployment default). Blue-green: run two full identical environments (blue = live, green = new). Switch traffic all at once, instant rollback by switching back. Canary: release to a small % of traffic first, watch metrics, then ramp up. Catches bad releases before they hit everyone.
topics.example:
Rolling:    v1 v1 v1 ▶ v2 v1 v1 ▶ v2 v2 v1 ▶ v2 v2 v2   (gradual)
Blue-green: blue (v1, live) │ green (v2, idle) ── flip LB ──▶ green live
Canary:     95% ▶ v1, 5% ▶ v2 ── metrics OK ──▶ 25% ▶ 50% ▶ 100%

Real world: blue-green on a payments API: deploy green, smoke-test it with zero live traffic, flip the load balancer in one shot, flip back instantly if anything looks wrong. Canary catches a bad release at 5% of users instead of 100%. K8s rolls by default: maxSurge and maxUnavailable tune the wave.

a: The concepts transfer 1:1 between clouds; interviews mostly test that you can name the managed service for each need. Managed Kubernetes: EKS (AWS) / GKE (GCP). Managed Postgres/MySQL: RDS and Aurora / Cloud SQL. Managed Redis: ElastiCache / Memorystore. Messaging: SQS for queues + SNS for fanout / Pub/Sub covers both. Object storage: S3 / Cloud Storage. Serverless containers: Fargate or App Runner / Cloud Run. Functions: Lambda / Cloud Functions.

Glue to know on both: IAM roles/service accounts with least privilege for workloads, VPC networking, CloudWatch / Cloud Monitoring for metrics and logs, ECR / Artifact Registry for container images. Learn one cloud deeply and map the names in the other.
topics.example:
need             AWS              GCP
kubernetes       EKS              GKE
Postgres/MySQL   RDS / Aurora     Cloud SQL
Redis            ElastiCache      Memorystore
queue + fanout   SQS + SNS        Pub/Sub
object storage   S3               Cloud Storage
containers       Fargate          Cloud Run
functions        Lambda           Cloud Functions

Real world: the same delivery-app stack runs on either cloud: API pods on EKS or GKE, orders in RDS or Cloud SQL, cart cache in ElastiCache or Memorystore, order.placed events on SNS+SQS or Pub/Sub, invoices in S3 or Cloud Storage, dashboards in CloudWatch or Cloud Monitoring plus Grafana. Learn one cloud deeply and map the names in the other.

a: Strangler fig pattern: put a gateway/facade in front of the monolith, then peel capabilities out one at a time into services. The gateway routes each request to either the monolith or the new service, so migration is gradual and reversible. Avoid a big-bang rewrite: it freezes features for months and usually fails.

Order of attack: start with a domain that is loosely coupled and changes often (high payoff, low risk). The hardest part is the database: give each extracted service its own schema/DB, sync data during transition with events or CDC (change data capture) and remove shared-table access last.
topics.example:
┌──▶ monolith (everything else)
gateway ───┤
           └──▶ payments-service (extracted, own DB)
     peel one capability at a time, route at the gateway

1 build payments-service with its own DB
2 gateway routes POST /payments to it
3 monolith reads payment status via the service API, not the old table
4 feature flag keeps both paths, easy revert
5 delete the monolith's payments module

Real world: named after the strangler fig tree that grows around a host until the host is gone. Shopify and Airbnb ran multi-year extractions this way: the monolith shrinks safely in production. The database is the hard part: sync with events or CDC during transition, remove shared-table access last.

a: The three pillars. Metrics: numeric time-series (request rate, error rate, latency, CPU). Cheap to store, great for dashboards and alerts, but no per-request detail. Logs: timestamped event records. Great for 'what exactly happened' on one request, expensive at scale if unstructured. Traces: follow a single request across services, showing where time went at each hop.
Together they answer: metrics say something is wrong, traces show where, logs show why.
topics.example:
metrics ─▶ something is wrong   (p99 latency spiked)
traces  ─▶ where                (400ms inside inventory-service)
logs    ─▶ why                  (DB query timed out, retrying)

Python:
  REQUEST_ERRORS.inc()                          # metric: one number goes up
  log.error("gateway timeout", trace_id=tid)    # log: the story, linked by trace id

Go:
  requestDuration.Observe(elapsed)        // metric: histogram sample
  ctx, span := tracer.Start(ctx, "charge")   // trace: one span per unit of work

Real world: alert fires on checkout p99 (Prometheus metric). The trace waterfall shows 400ms spent in inventory-service (Jaeger/Tempo). Logs at that timestamp show a timed-out DB query being retried (Loki/Elasticsearch). Three tools, one investigation.

a: Counter: only goes up (resets to 0 on restart). Total requests, total errors. Gauge: goes up and down. Current memory, active connections. Histogram: buckets observations (request duration) so percentiles can be computed at query time. Summary: like a histogram but computes quantiles client-side, harder to aggregate across instances.
topics.example:
counter    ▲ only up:       http_requests_total 1041 ▶ 1042
gauge      ▲▼ up and down:  active_connections 87 ▶ 62
histogram  buckets:         duration ≤0.1s: 900  ≤0.5s: 990  ≤1s: 999

PromQL:
  rate(http_requests_total[5m])   # counter ▶ requests per second
  histogram_quantile(0.99, rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m]))  # p99

Real world: a RED dashboard is two counters (rate, errors) plus one histogram (duration). Every Go service exports go_goroutines (gauge) out of the box. rate() handles counter resets after restarts, so counters stay safe to graph.

a: SLI (Service Level Indicator): the actual measured metric. Example: 99.95% of requests succeeded in the last 30 days. SLO (Service Level Objective): your internal target for that SLI. Example: aim for 99.9% availability. SLA (Service Level Agreement): the external contractual promise to customers, usually with a penalty if missed. Set looser than the internal SLO so there is buffer.
topics.example:
SLI  measured:  99.92% this month
SLO  internal:  99.90%  ← target (error budget: the 0.1% you may fail)
SLA  contract:  99.50%  ← penalty line (service credits)
     inside SLO and SLA here, but watch the trend

Budget math:
  99.9% monthly SLO = about 43 minutes of allowed downtime  # the error budget

Real world: AWS and GCP publish SLAs with service credits when breached. Google SRE teams freeze feature launches once the error budget is spent: reliability work only until it recovers. Pages tie to budget burn rate, not raw uptime.

a: Alert on symptoms users feel (high error rate, high latency, SLO burn rate), not on every internal cause. Cause-based alerts create fatigue and people start ignoring pages. Every alert must be actionable: if there is nothing to do when it fires, make it a dashboard panel, not a page.
Use burn-rate alerting for SLOs: alert faster when the error budget is burning fast (multi-window, multi-burn-rate), not on a single static threshold.
topics.example:
bad:   CPU > 80% for 1m        ─▶ pages at 3am, users fine, gets muted
good:  error rate > 5% for 5m  ─▶ users are hurting right now
good:  10% of monthly error budget burned in 1h ─▶ fast burn, page

PromQL:
  rate(errors_total[5m]) / rate(requests_total[5m]) > 0.05   # symptom, not cause

Real world: Google SRE burn-rate alerts page on fast burn and open a ticket on slow burn. The classic failure story: noisy CPU alerts get silenced, then a real outage scrolls past in the muted channel. Symptom alerts survive because every page means user pain.

a: In distributed systems, logs from dozens of services and instances must ship to one searchable place. You can't SSH into every box. Common stack: app writes structured JSON logs → shipper (Fluentd/Vector/Filebeat) → store and index (Elasticsearch/Loki) → view (Kibana/Grafana).
Structured logging (key-value JSON, not free text) is what makes logs queryable and correlatable across a whole request.
topics.example:
app instances ─▶ Vector/Filebeat ─▶ Elasticsearch/Loki ─▶ Kibana/Grafana
(every box ships, one place to search)

{"level":"error","service":"checkout","trace_id":"abc123","msg":"payment gateway timeout","user_id":42}

query trace_id=abc123 ─▶ every log line from every service for that one request

Python:
  log.error("gateway timeout", extra={"trace_id": tid})   # structured, not printf

Real world: grep over SSH dies at the second server. Loki keeps cost down by indexing labels only, not full text. ELK/Datadog bills explode when teams ship free-text debug logs: structure plus sampling is the fix.

a: A trace is one request's full journey across services. It is made of spans: one span per unit of work (a service call, a DB query), each with start/end time and a parent-child link. OpenTelemetry (OTel) is the current standard for emitting traces, metrics and logs consistently.
topics.example:
trace abc123 (waterfall)
 gateway   ├─────────────────────────────┤ 500ms
  auth     ├──┤ 50ms
  orders       ├─┤ 30ms
  payments        ├───────────────┤ 400ms  ← bottleneck

Python:
  with tracer.start_as_current_span("charge"):   # one span per unit of work
      charge_card()

Go:
  ctx, span := tracer.Start(ctx, "charge")   // child of the caller's span
  defer span.End()

Real world: OTel propagates context between services in the traceparent HTTP header, so spans from different services join into one trace. Jaeger, Tempo and Zipkin store and render the waterfalls. Uber built Jaeger to debug requests crossing thousands of microservices.

a: Grafana visualizes metrics (Prometheus, ClickHouse and others) as dashboards: graphs, gauges, tables. Usually organized around a service or an SLO so on-call sees health at a glance without querying by hand. Good dashboards follow USE for resources (Utilization, Saturation, Errors) or RED for services (Rate, Errors, Duration).
topics.example:
RED service dashboard (one glance: healthy or not?)
 ┌ Rate ─────┐ ┌ Errors ───┐ ┌ Duration ─────────┐
 │ 1.2k req/s│ │ 0.3%      │ │ p99 180ms         │
 └───────────┘ └───────────┘ └───────────────────┘

Panels behind it:
  rate(http_requests_total[5m])              # Rate
  histogram_quantile(0.99, ...)              # Duration p99

Real world: RED for services, USE for hosts (CPU utilization, run-queue saturation, hardware errors). On-call opens the service dashboard first, then jumps to traces from a panel link. Grafana alert rules can page straight from the same queries.

a: Message queue (RabbitMQ, SQS): each message is consumed by exactly one worker from the queue. Good for spreading work across a worker pool. Pub/Sub (Kafka topics, SNS): a message is broadcast to every subscriber independently. Good for fanning one event out to multiple unrelated consumers that each react to it.
topics.example:
Queue:   producer ─▶ [job|job|job] ─▶ one of N workers   (each job done once)
Pub/Sub: producer ─▶ topic ─┬▶ email-service      (every subscriber
                            └▶ analytics-service   gets its own copy)

Real world: image-resize jobs go to a queue, any one of 10 workers grabs each job. An order.placed event goes pub/sub: email-service and analytics-service each get their own copy. AWS: SQS is the queue, SNS is the fan-out. Kafka does both: one consumer group behaves like a queue, several groups behave like pub/sub.

a: At-most-once: message might be lost, never duplicated (fire and forget). At-least-once: guaranteed to arrive but maybe more than once. The most common default: brokers retry on ambiguous failures. Exactly-once: delivered and processed exactly one time. Very hard and expensive end-to-end. In practice you build effectively-once: at-least-once delivery plus idempotent processing.
topics.example:
at-most-once:  send ─▶ ?         (maybe lost, never duplicated)
at-least-once: send ─▶ ✓ ✓       (timeout ─▶ retry ─▶ duplicate possible)
exactly-once:  send ─▶ ✓         (needs dedup or transactions everywhere)

Real world: a consumer gets the same charge-card message twice after a network blip retry. Without idempotency that is a double charge. With an idempotency key the second copy is ignored: effectively-once. Kafka and SQS default to at-least-once. Metrics and logs often accept at-most-once: losing one data point is fine.

a: An operation is idempotent if running it many times has the same effect as running it once. Critical for safe retries in distributed systems: retries are inevitable (timeouts, network blips) and you often can't tell if the first attempt succeeded.
Common technique: an idempotency key (client-generated unique id per logical operation). The server remembers processed keys and returns the original result instead of re-executing a duplicate.
topics.example:
attempt 1 ─▶ POST /payments (Idempotency-Key: abc123) ─▶ charge, save key
retry     ─▶ same key ─▶ seen before ─▶ return saved result, no second charge

Python:
  cached = store.get(key)      # duplicate? replay the saved result
  if cached: return cached
  result = charge(card); store.set(key, result)

Real world: Stripe requires an Idempotency-Key header on payment POSTs. Naturally idempotent: SET status = 'paid', deleting a row. Not idempotent: counter = counter + 1, appending to a list: those need the key check.

a: Services communicate by emitting events ('order placed', 'user signed up') to a broker and other services react asynchronously, instead of calling each other directly.
