Decouples producers from consumers (a producer doesn't know who listens), improves resilience (a consumer being down doesn't block the producer) and scalability. Cost: flows are harder to trace and services are eventually consistent.
topics.example:
orders-service ─▶ broker: order.placed ─┬▶ inventory-service  (stock -1)
                                         ├▶ email-service      (confirmation)
                                         └▶ analytics-service
producer publishes and moves on: never waits, never knows who listens

Real world: checkout publishes order.placed and returns fast. If email-service is down for 5 minutes, emails arrive late but orders keep flowing: the broker holds the backlog. Tracing pain is real, so teams attach a correlation id to every event to follow one order across services.

a: A Kafka topic is split into partitions for parallelism. Each partition is an ordered append-only log. Order is guaranteed within a partition, not across the topic. A consumer group splits a topic's partitions between its instances (each partition is read by exactly one consumer in the group at a time). That is how Kafka scales consumption horizontally while keeping at-least-once processing per partition.
topics.example:
topic: orders (6 partitions)     consumer group (3 instances)
  p0, p1 ──────────────────────▶ consumer 1
  p2, p3 ──────────────────────▶ consumer 2
  p4, p5 ──────────────────────▶ consumer 3

producer.send('orders', key=order_id, value=event)  # same key ─▶ same partition

Real world: keying by order_id lands all of one order's events in one partition, so one consumer replays them in order. 6 partitions cap the group at 6 useful consumers: a 7th sits idle, which is why partition count is a scaling decision made up front. When a consumer dies the group rebalances and its partitions move to the survivors.

a: Consensus algorithms (Raft, Paxos) let a cluster of nodes agree on one value or state even when some nodes fail or messages are delayed. They are the backbone of leader election in etcd, Zookeeper and many distributed databases. Raft is popular because it is easier to understand than Paxos: nodes elect a leader, the leader replicates a log to followers and a value commits once a majority acknowledge it.
Eventual consistency (the contrast): no coordination overhead, replicas just converge over time. Much simpler and more available, but the app must tolerate briefly stale reads.
topics.example:
Raft (3 nodes): client ─▶ leader ─┬▶ follower ✓
                                  └▶ follower ✓
                commit once a majority (2 of 3) have written it

Real world: etcd stores Kubernetes cluster state with Raft: a write is acknowledged only after a majority stores it, so losing 1 of 3 nodes loses nothing and two conflicting leaders can't exist. DNS is the everyday eventual-consistency example: updates spread over TTLs and everyone converges eventually.

a: Prevents a failing downstream service from cascading failure through the whole system. States: Closed (normal, requests flow), Open (after too many failures, calls fail fast without touching the downstream service, giving it room to recover), Half-Open (after a cooldown, a few test requests probe whether it is healthy before fully closing).
topics.example:
Closed ──── 5 failures in a row ────▶ Open (fail fast, no calls)
   ▲                                     │ 30s cooldown
   └──── test call succeeds ──── Half-Open (let a few through)

Real world: orders-service calls a flaky recommendations-service. The circuit opens after 5 failures: for 30s orders-service instantly returns a fallback (empty recommendations) instead of burning threads on timeouts, so its own latency stays flat. Netflix Hystrix made the pattern famous; today resilience4j (Java) and gobreaker (Go) implement it.

a: A single ACID transaction can't span multiple services and databases, so a saga breaks a business transaction into a chain of local transactions, each with a compensating action that undoes it if a later step fails. Trades strict atomicity for eventual consistency plus explicit rollback logic.

Choreography: each service listens for events and reacts, no central coordinator. Simple, but the flow gets hard to trace as it grows. Orchestration: a central coordinator tells each service what to do next. Clearer flow, one more moving part.
topics.example:
reserve flight ─▶ reserve hotel ─▶ charge card ✗ fails
cancel flight  ◀─ cancel hotel  ◀─ compensate in reverse order

Real world: booking a trip touches three services and no single DB transaction covers them. The card charge fails, so the saga cancels the hotel then the flight. Orchestrated sagas run on tools like Temporal or AWS Step Functions; choreographed ones are just services reacting to each other's events.

a: Naive retries make outages worse: a struggling service gets hit by original traffic plus every client's retries (retry storm). Rules: retry only idempotent operations (or make them idempotent with keys), cap attempts (2-3), exponential backoff (1s, 2s, 4s) with jitter (randomness) so thousands of clients don't retry in synchronized waves.

Retry at ONE layer. If the client, the gateway and the service each retry 3x, one user click becomes 27 downstream calls. Also budget retries: stop retrying when overall error rate is high (retry budget/circuit breaker combo).
topics.example:
attempt 1 ─▶ fail ░wait 500ms░ attempt 2 ─▶ fail ░wait 1s░ attempt 3 ─▶ give up
with jitter: clients retry at 480ms, 530ms, 610ms... not one synchronized wave

Python:
  delay = base * 2**attempt + random.uniform(0, 0.3)   # exponential + jitter
  time.sleep(min(delay, max_delay))                    # always cap the wait

Go:
  delay := base * (1 << attempt)   // exponential backoff
  time.Sleep(delay + time.Duration(rand.Intn(300))*time.Millisecond)   // jitter

Real world: payment call times out: put an idempotency key on the charge, retry twice with backoff plus jitter, then fail and let the circuit breaker take over. AWS SDKs ship exponential backoff with jitter by default. The post-outage thundering herd (every client retrying at the same second) is exactly what jitter prevents.

a: Every network call needs an explicit timeout: the default in most clients is infinite and infinite waits pile up threads/goroutines until the service itself dies. A hanging dependency should cost you milliseconds of latency budget, not your worker pool.

Deadline propagation: the edge sets an overall budget (say 2s) and passes the remaining time down the chain (gRPC deadlines, Go context). Inner calls fail fast instead of doing work the caller already gave up on. Timeouts should shrink as you go deeper, never grow.
topics.example:
gateway (2s budget)
  └▶ orders-service (1.5s left)
       └▶ inventory (500ms left)   ← deadline shrinks going deeper

Python:
  requests.get(url, timeout=(0.5, 1.0))   # connect + read timeout, never infinite

Go:
  ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(ctx, 500*time.Millisecond)   // deadline rides the context
  resp, err := client.Do(req.WithContext(ctx))

Real world: without propagation inventory happily works 10s on a request the gateway already answered with 504 at 2s: wasted work nobody reads. gRPC forwards deadlines automatically across hops. Classic outage shape: an HTTP client with no default timeout hangs threads until the caller dies too.

a: Bulkhead: partition resources per dependency (separate connection pools, worker pools) so one slow downstream can only exhaust its own compartment, not the whole service. Named after ship compartments.

Load shedding: past a threshold, reject cheap and early (429/503 at the edge) instead of degrading for everyone. A bounded queue with rejection beats an unbounded queue that grows until OOM. Backpressure: consumers signal producers to slow down (bounded channels, Kafka consumer lag, TCP flow control) so pressure propagates instead of exploding somewhere.
Priority under stress: shed analytics and recommendations first, keep order placement and payment alive.
topics.example:
shared pool (200): slow recs eats all 200 threads ─▶ checkout dies too
bulkheads: [checkout 180] [recs 20] ─▶ only the 20 stall, checkout fine

Python:
  sem = asyncio.Semaphore(20)        # bulkhead: recs calls capped at 20
  async with sem: await get_recs()

Go:
  slots := make(chan struct{}, 20)   // bounded slots for the slow dependency
  select { case slots <- struct{}{}: default: return fallback }   // full: shed early

Real world: recommendations-service goes slow, its 20-thread bulkhead stalls, the fallback returns an empty list and checkout keeps its 180 threads. Netflix Hystrix made this pattern famous. Under stress shed analytics first and keep payments alive: a 429 at the edge beats an OOM in the core.

a: Rebalance: when a consumer joins/leaves a group, partitions are reassigned. Classic (eager) rebalance stops the whole group during reassignment: frequent deploys/crash-loops mean constant pauses. Cooperative (incremental) rebalancing only moves the partitions that must move. Rolling deploys of consumers trigger rebalances: know that.

Offsets: auto-commit on a timer can commit offsets for messages you have not finished processing (crash = message lost) or lose work done after last commit (crash = reprocessing). For at-least-once: process first, then commit manually. Consumer lag (latest offset minus committed) is THE health metric for consumers: alert on it.
Poison pill risk: a message that always crashes the consumer blocks its whole partition forever unless you catch, route to DLQ and commit past it.
topics.example:
group: [C1: p0 p1] [C2: p2 p3], then C3 joins
 eager:       everyone stops, ALL partitions reshuffle
 cooperative: only p1 moves to C3, the rest keep consuming

Python:
  for msg in consumer:
      process(msg)
      consumer.commit()   # at-least-once: process first, commit after

Go:
  session.MarkMessage(msg, "")   // sarama: mark offset after processing, not before

Real world: a rolling deploy of 10 consumer pods triggers a rebalance per restart: with eager rebalancing the group pauses 10 times. One malformed order-events message crash-loops a consumer: partition 3 lag grows unbounded while other partitions stay fine. Fix: 3 local attempts, produce to the DLQ, commit past it, alert on lag.

a: DLQ: after N failed processing attempts, move the message to a dead-letter topic/queue with error metadata (exception, attempt count, original topic/offset) instead of retrying forever or dropping silently. The main flow keeps moving; failures become inspectable.

Retry topics pattern (Kafka): retry-5m and retry-1h topics with delayed consumers give transient failures time to heal before the DLQ. Replay: after fixing the bug, re-produce DLQ messages to the original topic. This only works because consumers are idempotent: replay means duplicates by design.
A DLQ nobody monitors is a silent data-loss pit: alert on DLQ depth and age.
topics.example:
orders ─▶ consumer ── ok ─▶ done
             │ fail ×3
             ├▶ retry-5m ─▶ retry-1h         (transient errors heal)
             └▶ orders-dlq + error metadata   (alert on depth + age)

Python:
  except ProcessingError as e:
      if attempts >= 3:
          producer.send("orders-dlq", enrich(msg, e))   # then commit past it

Real world: payment webhook handler breaks on a new provider field: 40 messages land in webhooks-dlq, the alert fires, the main flow keeps moving. Deploy the fix, replay the 40, idempotency keys stop double-charging the two that half-succeeded. A DLQ nobody monitors is a silent data-loss pit.

a: In a distributed system, when a network partition happens, you must choose between Consistency (every read gets the latest write) and Availability (every request gets a response, even if not the latest data). You can't have both during the partition. Partition tolerance is basically mandatory for any real distributed system, so CAP is really a C-vs-A trade-off during a partition.

CP systems (traditional RDBMS with sync replication, Zookeeper, HBase): reject requests rather than return stale data. AP systems (Cassandra, DynamoDB default): stay available and reconcile later with eventual consistency.
topics.example:
Region 1 ══╳══ Region 2   (partition: link cut)

CP: minority side refuses writes ─▶ stays consistent, partly down
AP: both sides keep accepting    ─▶ stays up, conflicts merged later

Real world: bank ledgers pick CP: better to reject a request than show a wrong balance. Amazon's cart is the classic AP story: never block add-to-cart, merge carts after the partition heals. Zookeeper is CP: lose quorum and it stops answering rather than lie.

a: Strong consistency: every read sees the latest committed write, everywhere, immediately. Simplest to reason about, costliest to scale globally. Eventual consistency: replicas converge over time, but a read right after a write can return stale data. Much easier to scale, needs conflict-resolution thinking. Causal consistency sits in between: causally related operations are seen in the same order by everyone, unrelated ones can differ.
topics.example:
write new photo ─▶ replica A (updated)
                 └▶ replica B (old for ~100ms, still replicating)

Strong:   read waits or routes to latest ─▶ always the new photo
Eventual: read B in that window ─▶ old photo briefly

Real world: your own profile edit should be read-your-writes (route that user to the primary). A like counter can be eventual: nobody notices a 1s-late count. DynamoDB lets you choose per read: eventually consistent by default, strongly consistent for double the cost.

a: Vertical scaling: make one machine bigger (more CPU/RAM). Simple, no architecture change, but it has a hard ceiling and stays a single point of failure. Horizontal scaling: add more machines and spread load with a load balancer. Near-unlimited ceiling and better fault tolerance, but the app must be stateless (or push state to a shared store like Redis or the DB) so any instance can handle any request.
topics.example:
Vertical:   [ 4 CPU ] ─▶ [ 64 CPU ]     (same 1 box, just bigger)
Horizontal: LB ─▶ [app] [app] [app]     (more boxes, any can serve)

Real world: sessions kept in local memory break horizontal scaling: the next request lands on another instance and the user is logged out. Move sessions to Redis and every instance becomes interchangeable. Scaling up first is fine: one strong box serves thousands of QPS. Kubernetes HPA is horizontal scaling on autopilot: add pods when CPU climbs.

a: Layer caches close to where they save the most work: browser cache → CDN (static assets) → application-layer cache (Redis, for computed or DB results) → the database's own buffer pool.
Key decisions: what to cache, TTL and invalidation strategy (time-based expiry vs explicit invalidation on write vs versioned keys that just go stale naturally).
topics.example:
request ─▶ browser ─▶ CDN edge ─▶ Redis ─▶ Postgres
            0ms hit     ~20ms       ~1ms     ~30ms + load
            each layer stops a share of traffic before the next

Real world: a product page serves images from the CDN, caches the rendered fragment in Redis for 60s (slightly stale price, massive read cut) and keeps the DB indexed so misses are still fast. News sites cache the whole homepage HTML at the CDN for ~30s to absorb traffic spikes millions strong.

a: Fixed window: count requests per fixed time bucket (per minute). Simple, but bursts slip through at window edges (2x the limit right at the boundary). Sliding window: smooths that by weighting the previous window. Token bucket: tokens refill at a steady rate, each request takes one. Allows short bursts up to bucket size while holding a long-term average. Leaky bucket: requests queue and drain at a constant rate, smoothing bursts entirely.
topics.example:
Fixed window edge: |......xxxxx|xxxxx......|  10 at 0:59 + 10 at 1:00 = 20 in 2s
Token bucket (10, refill 1/s): ●●●●●●●●●● burst 10 ─▶ then steady 1/s

Real world: token bucket is the API default: Stripe and AWS let clients burst then settle to a steady rate. Nginx limit_req is a leaky bucket: excess requests queue or drop. Whichever algorithm, the contract to the client is 429 plus a Retry-After header.

a: Range-based sharding: split by value ranges (user_id 1-1M on shard A). Simple, but hot shards appear when traffic isn't uniform. Hash-based sharding: hash the shard key to pick a shard. Spreads load evenly, but cross-shard range queries get harder and resharding is painful. Directory-based: a lookup service maps keys to shards. Flexible, but the directory becomes a dependency and possible bottleneck.
Also pick a shard key that keeps related data together (shard by tenant_id in a multi-tenant app) to avoid expensive cross-shard joins.
topics.example:
Range: ids 1-1M ─▶ A    1M-2M ─▶ B    (all new users hit B: hot shard)
Hash:  hash(id) % 4 ─▶ A │ B │ C │ D   (even spread, no range scans)

Real world: a multi-tenant SaaS shards by tenant_id so one customer's queries always stay on one shard: no cross-shard joins in normal traffic. New-signup growth makes range sharding run hot on the newest shard. Consistent hashing exists because plain hash resharding moves almost every key; with a hash ring, adding a node moves only ~1/N of them.

topics.q: Reverse Proxy vs Load Balancer vs API Gateway
a: Reverse proxy: sits in front of backend servers and forwards client requests to them (plus TLS termination, caching, compression). Nginx is the classic. Load balancer: a reverse proxy whose main job is spreading traffic across identical instances. API Gateway: a reverse proxy specialized for APIs. It adds auth, rate limiting, routing to different microservices and request transformation in one entry point.
topics.example:
client ─▶ API Gateway (checks JWT, rate limits)
             ├─ /orders/*   ─▶ LB ─▶ orders pods
             └─ /payments/* ─▶ LB ─▶ payments pods

Real world: the same binary can play all three roles: plain Nginx is a reverse proxy, give it upstreams and it is a load balancer. Kong and AWS API Gateway handle the API tier (auth, quotas, routing). In Kubernetes the Ingress sits at the edge while each Service load-balances its pods.

a: Interviewers often want quick capacity math to sanity-check a design, not exact numbers. Know rough orders of magnitude: 1 day ≈ 86,400s (~100k for quick math), memory access ~100ns, SSD read ~100μs, network round trip within a region ~0.5-1ms, cross-continent ~100-150ms.

Standard approach: estimate DAU/QPS → estimate read:write ratio and peak factor (often 2-3x average) → estimate storage growth per day and year → sanity check against a single machine's typical capacity (thousands of QPS, TBs of disk) to decide if you actually need to distribute.
topics.example:
10M DAU × 10 req/day = 100M req/day
100M ÷ ~100k s ≈ 1,150 req/s average ─▶ ×3 peak ≈ 3,500 req/s
storage: 100M × 1KB/day ≈ 100GB/day ≈ 36TB/year

Real world: handy shortcuts: 1M requests/day ≈ 12 req/s, 1 day ≈ 100k seconds. A single well-indexed Postgres primary with read replicas handles thousands of QPS, so this math usually ends with 'load-balance the app tier, no shard yet'. Interviewers grade the method, not the decimals.

topics.q: Interview Framework (How to Attack Any Design)
a: Fixed order, say it out loud: 1) Requirements: functional + non-functional (scale, latency, consistency needs). 2) Back-of-envelope: DAU, QPS, storage. 3) API sketch: main endpoints. 4) Data model: core tables/entities. 5) High-level diagram: services, DB, cache, queue. 6) Deep dive where the interviewer steers. 7) Bottlenecks: single points of failure, hot spots, what breaks at 10x.
Senior signal: state trade-offs explicitly ('I choose eventual consistency here because...') and name what you are NOT building. Do not jump to microservices and Kafka before justifying them.
topics.example:
1 Requirements ─▶ 2 Numbers ─▶ 3 API ─▶ 4 Data model
                                                │
    7 Bottlenecks ◀─ 6 Deep dive ◀─ 5 High-level diagram

Quick math you say out loud:
  1M DAU × 2 orders = 2M orders/day ≈ 23 QPS average, ~100 QPS peak (4-5x)
  2M × 2 KB per order ≈ 4 GB/day: one Postgres handles this fine

Bad open: 'So we'll have a load balancer, some microservices and Kafka.'
Good open: 'Who are the users, how many orders per day and can order placement ever be down? That decides how much I invest in availability.'

a: Core services: order-service (order state machine: placed → accepted → preparing → picked_up → delivered / cancelled), restaurant-service (menu, availability), dispatch-service (assign riders), payments, notifications. Orders and payments in Postgres (ACID). Menu/catalog cacheable in Redis. Events (order.placed, order.accepted) on a broker so services stay decoupled.

Rider tracking: riders ping location every few seconds. That write volume does not belong in Postgres: push to Redis (geo sets) or a time-series store, fan out to the customer over WebSocket/SSE. Dispatch: match by proximity (geohash / Redis GEO), rider load and restaurant prep time.

Peak handling (lunch and dinner rush): autoscale stateless services (HPA), queue order processing so bursts buffer instead of dropping, degrade gracefully: ETA and tracking can be stale, order placement and payment must not fail.
topics.example:
POST /orders ─▶ order-service ─▶ Postgres: order + outbox event (1 tx)
                    │
             broker (order.paid)
             ├─▶ restaurant tablet accepts
             ├─▶ dispatch ─▶ Redis GEO: nearest free rider
             └─▶ notifications
 customer ◀══ WebSocket live ETA ══ rider GPS pings ─▶ Redis (not Postgres)

Numbers to drop: 10K active riders pinging every 3s ≈ 3.3K writes/s. That is why GPS goes to Redis geo sets, not Postgres. Dinner rush is 5-10x baseline: queue order processing so bursts buffer, autoscale the stateless services.

Retellable rule: order placement and payment must never fail; ETA and tracking may go stale. Uber and Careem degrade exactly this way under load. Payment charge carries an idempotency key so a retry never double-charges.

a: Requirements first: per-user or per-IP, limit shape (steady rate vs bursts allowed), global or per-instance, what happens on breach (429 + Retry-After).

Standard answer: token bucket per key stored in Redis, so all API instances share state. Check-and-decrement must be atomic: use a Lua script (read count, refill by elapsed time, decrement, set TTL in one call), otherwise two instances race. Local in-memory limiter in front as a cheap first layer is a nice bonus point.
Mention failure mode: if Redis is down, fail open (allow traffic) for availability or fail closed for protection. Say which and why for this API.
topics.example:
request ─▶ any API instance ─▶ Redis Lua script (atomic):
              refill by elapsed time ─▶ take 1 token
              │ token available: pass, X-RateLimit-Remaining: 7
              └ bucket empty: 429 + Retry-After: 2

Key rl:user:42, bucket 20, refill 10/s: bursts up to 20 allowed, steady 10/s after. Lua matters because read + refill + decrement happen in one call: two instances cannot race. Payment endpoints get a stricter separate bucket than reads.

Real world: Stripe and GitHub return exactly these rate-limit headers. Redis down? Fail open for a public read API (availability), fail closed for login or payments (protection). Saying which and why is the senior point.

a: Ingest: services publish notification events to a queue, never call SMS/email providers inline (slow, flaky third parties must not sit in the request path). Workers consume, apply user preferences and quiet hours, pick channel (push, SMS, email), call the provider adapter.

Reliability: retries with backoff per provider, DLQ for poison messages, idempotency key per notification so retries never double-send. Priority queues: OTP beats marketing. Dedup/collapse: 10 likes become one 'You have 10 likes' push.
Scale reads: delivery status and unread counts in Redis; full history in DB, partitioned by user.
topics.example:
event ─▶ queue ─▶ worker ─▶ prefs + quiet hours ─▶ adapter (FCM / SMS / email)
                     │ provider 5xx: retry 3x with backoff
                     └ still failing: DLQ + alert

Why the queue: SMS and email providers are slow flaky third parties, so they must never sit in the request path. Idempotency key per notification (order-123-delivered) means a retry never double-sends. Templates render in the user's language (AR/EN).

Retellable details: the OTP queue outranks the marketing queue (priority). 10 likes collapse into one 'You have 10 likes' push (dedup). Chat apps keep unread counts in Redis and partition full history by user.

a: Classic warm-up. Core: generate a short code for a long URL, redirect fast. Code generation options: base62-encode an auto-increment ID (simple, predictable), pre-generated key pool, or hash + collision check. For distributed ID generation without a single counter: Snowflake-style IDs or per-node ranges.

Read path dominates (100:1 or more): cache code → URL in Redis, CDN can even cache redirects. 301 (permanent, browsers cache, less analytics) vs 302 (temporary, every hit reaches you, full analytics): pick 302 if click tracking matters.
Storage math: 100M URLs × ~500 bytes ≈ 50 GB. Fits one Postgres with replicas: say that instead of sharding reflexively.
topics.example:
Write: POST /shorten ─▶ ID from node's range ─▶ base62 ─▶ store ─▶ short URL
Read:  GET /abc123 ─▶ Redis ── hit: 302 redirect
                        │ miss
                        └─▶ Postgres ─▶ backfill cache (TTL)
       click event ─▶ queue ─▶ async analytics

Numbers: 100M URLs × 500 bytes ≈ 50 GB: one Postgres with replicas, no sharding needed. Reads beat writes 100:1, so the cache does the real work.

Retellable trade-off: 301 gets cached by browsers (fast, loses analytics), 302 hits your server every time (full click tracking). Bitly-style services pick 302 because clicks are the product.

a: A fixed order beats intuition under pressure: 1) Scope the blast radius: one endpoint or everything, one region or all, all users or a subset. 2) Check what changed: deploys, config flags, traffic shifts, dependency releases. Most incidents follow a change. 3) Read RED metrics (rate, errors, duration) for the service, then USE (utilization, saturation, errors) for its resources. 4) Follow one failing request with a trace, then read its logs. 5) Mitigate first (rollback, scale, flag off), root-cause later.
Say the mitigation-first part out loud in interviews: restoring service beats finding the bug. Rollback is a valid answer, not an admission of defeat.
topics.example:
scope blast radius ▶ what changed? ▶ RED metrics ▶ one trace ▶ mitigate

Commands:
  kubectl rollout history deploy/api   # what shipped recently
  kubectl rollout undo deploy/api      # mitigate first, root-cause later

Real world: checkout error rate hits 8% at 12:03. Deploy log shows a release at 11:58. Roll back first, confirm recovery at 12:07, then diff the release to find the bug. Total impact: 9 minutes. The wrong version: debugging live while users keep failing for an hour.

a: First split: p99 up while p50 flat means a subset of requests is slow: queueing, lock contention, one slow shard or dependency, GC pauses, cold cache. Both up means systemic: saturation, downstream slowdown or a bad deploy.

Checklist: RED dashboard to find which endpoint; a trace to see where the time goes (own CPU vs downstream call vs DB); connection pool wait time; DB slow query log; cache hit rate; GC pause metrics; retry amplification (a slow dependency plus retries multiplies its own load).
topics.example:
p99 up, p50 flat ─▶ a subset is slow: locks, one shard, GC, cold cache
p99 up, p50 up   ─▶ systemic: saturation, downstream, bad deploy

Find lock waits:
  SELECT pid, wait_event, query FROM pg_stat_activity
  WHERE wait_event_type = 'Lock';

Real world: trace shows 1.8s of a 2s request inside one DB call. pg_stat_activity: dozens of queries waiting on the same row lock. Root cause: a new cron job runs a long transaction updating hot rows. Kill the job, p99 recovers instantly. Permanent fix: run it off-peak and commit in small chunks.

a: Order of checks: 1) pg_stat_activity: what runs right now, is one query piled up many times. 2) pg_stat_statements: top queries by total time. 3) EXPLAIN the top offender: a seq scan on a big table usually means a missing or unusable index (function on an indexed column, implicit cast, stale statistics). 4) Connection count: hundreds of active backends burn CPU on context switching even when each query is fine. 5) Autovacuum health: bloat and outdated stats push the planner into bad plans.
Quick mitigations: kill the offending query, CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY for the missing index, route reads to a replica, cache the hot query in Redis.
topics.example:
pg_stat_activity ▶ pg_stat_statements ▶ EXPLAIN top query ▶ connections ▶ vacuum
 (running now)      (top by total time)    (seq scan? bad plan?)

SELECT query, calls, total_exec_time FROM pg_stat_statements
ORDER BY total_exec_time DESC LIMIT 5;   -- who burns the CPU
CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_orders_user ON orders(user_id);   -- no write lock

Real world: an ORM upgrade silently dropped eager loading: 50k identical single-row SELECTs per minute (N+1 flood). Each query is cheap, together they eat all CPU. pg_stat_statements shows calls exploding while mean time stays tiny: that signature = N+1. Fix: restore the eager load.

a: Symptoms: RSS climbs steadily under flat traffic, restarts fix it temporarily, Kubernetes shows OOMKilled (exit code 137) restart loops that look like random crashes. Confirm leak vs load: memory must grow while traffic does not.

Method: take two heap profiles at different times and diff them (pprof in Go, heap snapshots in Node, jmap + MAT in Java). Usual suspects: unbounded in-memory caches or maps, listeners and goroutines never cleaned up on error paths, per-connection buffers, globals holding request-scoped data.
topics.example:
RSS under flat traffic: ▁▂▃▄▅▆▇   restart ▶ drops ▶ climbs again = leak

Go (diff two heap profiles):
  curl :6060/debug/pprof/heap > h1.prof      # snapshot now
  go tool pprof -diff_base h1.prof h2.prof   # 10 min later: what grew

Real world: Go service where goroutine count in pprof grows forever. Each request spawns a goroutine waiting on a channel never closed on the error path. Fix: pass a context and select on ctx.Done() so the goroutine exits when the request dies. Kubernetes face of the same bug: OOMKilled (exit 137) restart loops.

a: Lag grows when produce rate exceeds consume rate. First question: spike (will drain on its own) or steady growth (never drains without action). Then check consumer health: crash loops, rebalance storms, one stuck partition (poison message), or a slow downstream dependency inside the handler.

Fix by cause: scale consumers (in Kafka this only helps up to the partition count), DLQ the poison message and commit past it, batch the slow downstream call, raise partition count for future headroom, apply backpressure upstream if producers can slow down.
topics.example:
produce 5k/s ─▶ [ queue lag ▁▂▃▅▇ ] ─▶ consume 3k/s
 spike: drains on its own     steady growth: never drains without action

Kafka:
  kafka-consumer-groups --describe --group orders   # per-partition lag

Real world: one partition lagging, the rest fine → poison message crash-looping its consumer. DLQ it and commit past it, lag drains in minutes. All partitions lagging evenly → the payment API inside the handler got 300ms slower. Batch the calls or scale consumers (helps only up to the partition count).

a: The pattern: one dependency slows down, callers' threads and connections pile up waiting on it, their pools exhaust, their own callers start failing and the whole system browns out. Retries and aggressive health-check evictions amplify every step.

Triage: find the deepest unhealthy service (the first to degrade in the timeline), not the loudest alert: alerts fire top-down but causes live bottom-up. Mitigate: shed load at the edge, open circuit breakers or flag the feature off, scale the true bottleneck, temporarily disable retries.
Prevention vocabulary to name: timeouts with deadline propagation, circuit breakers, bulkheads, load shedding, jittered retries, graceful degradation.
topics.example:
DB slow ─▶ svc A pool full ─▶ svc B threads wait ─▶ edge 5xx
 alerts fire top-down ▲         cause lives bottom-up ▼

Triage rule: walk the timeline to the first service that degraded, not the loudest alert.

Real world: recommendations DB slows → recommendations-service saturates → product-page calls it with no timeout and exhausts its thread pool → homepage goes down. One 200ms timeout plus an empty-list fallback at the top restores everything except recommendations while the DB is fixed.

a: Sorted input + target or pair → two pointers or binary search. Contiguous subarray/substring with a constraint → sliding window. Counting, duplicates, complements → hash map. Top-K or K-th largest → heap. All paths, permutations, nested choices → DFS/backtracking. Shortest path or level-by-level → BFS. Overlapping subproblems with optimal substructure → dynamic programming. Prerequisites or ordering → topological sort. Connectivity and grouping → union-find.
Interviews reward naming the pattern before coding: 'longest substring with at most K distinct characters is a sliding window with a frequency map.' It shows recognition, not luck.
topics.example:
sorted + pair        ─▶ two pointers / binary search
subarray constraint  ─▶ sliding window
counts, complements  ─▶ hash map
top-K                ─▶ heap
all combinations     ─▶ DFS / backtracking
fewest steps         ─▶ BFS
ordering with deps   ─▶ topological sort

Python (two sum, unsorted):
  seen = {}
  for i, x in enumerate(nums):
      if target - x in seen: return [seen[target - x], i]   # complement seen before
      seen[x] = i

Same problem on a sorted array: two pointers from both ends, O(1) space. The sorted property decides the pattern.

Real world: rate limiters are sliding windows, autocomplete top suggestions is a heap, build systems and job schedulers with dependencies run topological sort.

a: Two pointers, three flavors: converging ends on sorted data (pair sum, container with most water), fast/slow (cycle detection, middle of a linked list), read/write (in-place dedup or removal). Sliding window: grow the right edge, shrink the left edge while the constraint is broken, keep window state in counters or a frequency map.
Why they are O(n): each element enters and leaves the window (or is passed by a pointer) at most once. No restart from scratch per position.
topics.example:
Longest substring without repeats: abcabcbb
  a b c a b c b b
  L───R             window abc unique: grow R
      L───R         duplicate a: shrink L until unique again

Python:
  seen = set(); L = best = 0
  for R, ch in enumerate(s):
      while ch in seen: seen.remove(s[L]); L += 1   # shrink on duplicate
      seen.add(ch); best = max(best, R - L + 1)     # grow + record

O(n): every char enters the window once and leaves at most once.

Real world: TCP flow control slides a window over the byte stream. Log scanners answer 'most errors in any 5 minute span' with a time-based window. Fast/slow pointers detect cycles in linked structures (Floyd's algorithm).

topics.q: BFS vs DFS vs Binary Search Decisions
a: BFS: shortest path in unweighted graphs, minimum number of steps, level-order processing. Queue plus a visited set. DFS: exhaustive exploration, path existence, backtracking, tree recursion, topological sort. Watch recursion depth on large inputs.

Binary search is not just for sorted arrays: any monotonic yes/no question ('does capacity X suffice?') can be binary searched on the answer space. If feasibility only flips once as X grows, binary search the smallest feasible X.
topics.example:
BFS: level by level (queue)     DFS: dive deep, backtrack (stack)
 shortest steps, min moves       all paths, cycles, topo sort

Binary search on the answer (monotonic feasibility):
 capacity:  no no no YES YES YES ─▶ find the first YES in O(log range)

Python (min ship capacity in D days):
  lo, hi = max(w), sum(w)
  while lo < hi:
      mid = (lo + hi) // 2
      if days_needed(mid) <= D: hi = mid   # feasible: try smaller
      else: lo = mid + 1                   # too small: go bigger

Real world: BFS = fewest hops in a social graph or network route. DFS = dependency resolution and cycle detection in service call graphs. Binary search on the answer = capacity planning: smallest worker count that keeps latency under the SLO.

a: Rules of thumb: roughly 10^8 simple operations per second. n ≤ 20 → exponential/backtracking is fine. n ≤ 5,000 → O(n²) is fine. n around 10^5 to 10^6 → you need O(n log n) or O(n). Sorting is O(n log n); heap push/pop O(log n); hash operations O(1) average; binary search O(log n).
Space counts too: recursion depth is stack space and many DP tables compress to two rows.
Practice reps live in vizly DSA Quest; this section is recall only.
topics.example:
What survives 1 second (~10^8 simple ops):
 n ≤ 20     ─▶ 2^n backtracking OK
 n ≤ 5,000  ─▶ O(n²) OK
 n ≥ 10^5   ─▶ need O(n log n) or O(n)

n = 10^5 nested loop = 10^10 ops: timeout, no code needed to know it.

Python:
  nums.sort()            # O(n log n)
  heapq.heappush(h, x)   # O(log n)
  x in seen              # set/dict lookup: O(1) average

Real world: the same math sizes production code: an O(n²) dedup that passed review at 1K rows melts at 1M. Postgres chooses hash join vs nested loop with the same estimates.

a: A goroutine is a lightweight thread managed by the Go runtime: a few KB of stack, multiplexed onto OS threads by the scheduler (M:N), so hundreds of thousands are fine. Started with the go keyword.

Channels are typed pipes between goroutines: 'share memory by communicating, not communicate by sharing memory.' Unbuffered channel: send blocks until a receiver is ready (a synchronization point). Buffered channel: send blocks only when the buffer is full. close(ch) signals no more values; range over a channel reads until it is closed.
topics.example:
go keyword: main ─▶ go f() runs concurrently (~2KB stack, scheduler maps M:N)
channel:    producer ──▶ [ jobs buffer 100 ] ──▶ 10 workers

Go:
  jobs := make(chan Job, 100)   // buffered channel
  for i := 0; i < 10; i++ {
      go func() { for j := range jobs { process(j) } }()   // worker pool
  }
  close(jobs)   // no more jobs: workers' range loops end

Real world: every request in a Go HTTP server runs in its own goroutine, no thread pool tuning. A crawler fetches 10,000 URLs with 10 workers reading one jobs channel. Docker and Kubernetes are Go programs juggling thousands of goroutines this way.

a: select waits on multiple channel operations and runs whichever is ready first: the core tool for timeouts, cancellation and multiplexing. context.Context carries deadlines and cancellation down a call chain; every blocking call should respect ctx.Done(). Cancel a parent context and everything below it stops.

sync package: Mutex/RWMutex for shared state, WaitGroup to wait for a set of goroutines, Once for one-time init. errgroup (golang.org/x/sync) combines WaitGroup with error propagation and context cancellation.
topics.example:
select: whichever channel is ready first wins
  case msg := <-ch:      // data arrived
  case <-ctx.Done():     // timeout or cancel fired

Go:
  ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(r.Context(), 2*time.Second)
  defer cancel()
  row := db.QueryRowContext(ctx, query)   // client gone or 2s up: query stops

Real world: gRPC propagates context across services: one client timeout cancels the whole downstream call tree. errgroup fans out 3 API calls and the first error cancels the siblings. Handlers that ignore ctx leak goroutines every time a client disconnects.

a: Go interfaces are satisfied implicitly: any type with the matching methods implements the interface, no 'implements' keyword. This keeps packages decoupled: define the interface where it is used (the consumer), not where it is implemented.
Idioms: keep interfaces small (io.Reader has one method), 'accept interfaces, return structs.' There is no inheritance: reuse comes from struct embedding (composition).
topics.example:
consumer defines the interface:
  orders pkg ─▶ Notifier { Notify(ctx, msg) error }
  EmailNotifier ✓   SlackNotifier ✓   (matching methods = implements, no keyword)

Go:
  type Notifier interface { Notify(ctx context.Context, msg string) error }
  func NewService(n Notifier) *Service   // accept interfaces, return structs

Real world: io.Reader has one method, so files, sockets, gzip streams and bytes.Buffer all plug into the same code. Tests hand-write a fake Notifier struct, no mocking framework needed. http.Handler is one interface and every Go web framework builds on it.

a: Errors are plain values returned as the last result and checked with if err != nil. No exceptions for normal control flow. Wrap errors with context: fmt.Errorf("fetch user %d: %w", id, err); inspect the chain with errors.Is (sentinel match) and errors.As (type match).
panic/recover is only for truly unrecoverable states, never for expected failures like a missing row. defer runs cleanup on the way out (close files, unlock mutexes) in LIFO order.
topics.example:
sql.ErrNoRows (driver)
  └─ wrap: fmt.Errorf("get user 42: %w", err)
       └─ errors.Is ─▶ domain ErrUserNotFound ─▶ handler returns 404

Go:
  if err != nil { return fmt.Errorf("fetch user %d: %w", id, err) }  // add context, keep chain
  if errors.Is(err, sql.ErrNoRows) { return ErrUserNotFound }        // translate to domain error

Real world: wrapped errors make log lines read like a story: 'handle order 9: charge card: gateway timeout'. Each layer translates upward: driver error to domain error to HTTP status. Web frameworks recover() per request so one panicking handler doesn't kill the server.

a: A slice is a small header (pointer, length, capacity) over a backing array: two slices can share the same array, so a write through one is visible in the other. append may reallocate, so always assign the result back. Maps are not safe for concurrent writes: guard with a mutex or use sync.Map.

Runtime: concurrent mark-and-sweep GC tuned for sub-millisecond pauses, GOMAXPROCS controls parallelism. Go compiles to one static binary, which is why Go container images are tiny (FROM scratch works).
topics.example:
backing array: [10][20][30][40]   a = full slice, cap 4
b := a[:2] ─▶ same array
b = append(b, 99) ─▶ [10][20][99][40]   ← a[2] silently overwritten

Go:
  b := a[:2]
  b = append(b, 99)                        // spare capacity: writes into a's array
  c := make([]int, len(a)); copy(c, a)     // safe independent copy

Real world: classic prod bug: slice a cached response, append to the sub-slice, corrupt the cache. Concurrent map writes crash the process (fatal error: concurrent map writes): guard with a mutex or sync.Map. Go builds one static binary, so FROM scratch Docker images are a few MB.

a: STAR: Situation (one sentence of context), Task (what YOU owned), Action (what YOU did: 70% of the answer, say 'I' not 'we'), Result (quantified outcome + what you learned). Keep the whole answer 2-3 minutes.

Prepare 6-8 stories before interviews and map them to the usual questions: hardest technical problem, conflict with a colleague, failure/mistake, tight deadline, mentoring someone, disagreeing with a decision, leading without authority. One strong story can serve multiple questions from different angles.
Quantify results: '82M requests/month', 'cut p99 from 800ms to 120ms', 'onboarding time from 2 weeks to 3 days'. Numbers make stories credible and memorable.
topics.example:
S ─ Situation: 1 sentence of context
T ─ Task: what YOU owned
A ─ Action: what YOU did, 70% of the answer, say 'I'
R ─ Result: a number + a lesson

Sample ('tell me about a production issue you owned'):
 S: checkout errors spiked at peak.
 T: I was on call and led the incident.
 A: I checked the RED dashboard, traced it to connection pool exhaustion, applied a bulkhead and capped the pools, wrote the postmortem.
 R: 40 minutes of impact. The incident class never recurred and the fix became a platform default.

Retell one strong story from different angles (failure, deadline, conflict): it serves many questions. Numbers do the convincing.

a: Senior roles are expected to mentor, so have concrete answers ready. Mentoring: pair on real tickets rather than lecture, give the junior a slightly-too-big task with a safety net, do regular 1:1s, measure success by them not needing you anymore.

Code review philosophy: review for correctness, tests and design first, style last (linters own style). Distinguish blocking issues from nitpicks explicitly ('nit:' prefix). Comment on the code, never the person; ask questions instead of commanding ('what happens if this times out?'). Big PRs get a synchronous walkthrough instead of 200 comments.
Senior signal: you raise the team's level (docs, patterns, onboarding), not just your own output.
topics.example:
People-question shape:
 1. diagnose privately (find the real gap)
 2. agree a plan together
 3. pair on it
 4. measure over time
 5. escalate only after that

Sample ('a junior keeps submitting buggy PRs, what do you do?'):
 'First I pair with them privately to find the real gap: testing habits or domain knowledge. We agree a pre-PR checklist, I pair-write tests on their next feature and we track a month of PRs. The manager only hears about it if nothing improves.'

Review lines that land well: 'nit:' prefix for non-blockers, 'what happens if this times out?' instead of 'this is wrong', a walkthrough call for big PRs instead of 200 comments.

a: Disagreement pattern interviewers want: you argued with data and prototypes, not volume; you genuinely listened to the other side; a decision got made (by you, consensus or escalation); then you committed fully even if it wasn't your choice: disagree and commit.

Ambiguity (a standard senior-role requirement): show a bias for reversible action. Timebox research, write a one-page proposal with options and a recommendation, pick the reversible option when unsure, set a checkpoint to revisit. Never 'I waited for someone to decide.'
Escalation is not failure: escalating a stuck decision with a clear write-up of both options is a senior move.
topics.example:
Disagreement skeleton:
 data ▶ listen ▶ decide ▶ commit (even when it wasn't your choice)

Ambiguity skeleton:
 timebox research ▶ one-pager with options + recommendation ▶ pick the reversible option ▶ set a checkpoint

Sample: 'I pushed for Postgres, a teammate wanted MongoDB. I wrote a one-pager comparing both against our access patterns and load tested the riskiest query. We picked Postgres, but their schema-churn concern was valid, so we added a jsonb column for the volatile attributes. Shipped on time. Both of us owned the result.'

Escalating a stuck decision with a clear write-up of both options is a senior move, not a failure.

topics.q: Go, Ruby/Rails, Java/JVM, Python Quick Notes
a: Go: compiled to one static binary, goroutines make high concurrency cheap (no GIL/GVL equivalent), low memory footprint and fast startup: the default pick for new microservices, proxies and infra tooling. Small language by design: little magic, fast onboarding, but more boilerplate than Rails/Django. The dedicated Go section above covers it in depth.

Ruby/Rails: MRI has a GVL (global VM lock), so one process runs one thread of Ruby at a time; scaling is multi-process (Puma workers) plus threads for I/O. Rails = convention over configuration: ActiveRecord ORM (watch N+1: use includes), migrations, Sidekiq (Redis-backed) for background jobs. Many delivery and e-commerce companies still run a Rails monolith, so expect at least respect-level questions.

Java/JVM: real OS threads (virtual threads since 21 for cheap concurrency), generational GC (G1 default, ZGC for low pause), JIT warms up hot paths. Spring Boot: DI container, @Transactional, heavy but battle-tested for large teams.

Python: GIL means threads don't help CPU-bound work: use multiprocessing or async I/O (FastAPI/asyncio) for concurrency. Type hints + mypy for large codebases. Common in tooling, data and ML services around a Go/Java core.
Interview stance: 'strongest in Go/Node, productive quickly in the others and the fundamentals (DB, HTTP, testing, design) transfer.' Then prove it with these specifics.
topics.example:
One-line map:
 Go     ─ static binary, cheap goroutines, infra default
 Rails  ─ GVL, multi-process scaling (Puma workers), convention magic
 JVM    ─ real threads (virtual since 21), tuned GC, Spring DI
 Python ─ GIL, async or multiprocessing, glue + ML services

Sample ('Rails app is slow under load, what do you check?'):
 'N+1 queries in the log (bullet gem), missing indexes, too few Puma workers fighting the GVL, external calls without timeouts holding request threads, then fragment and query caching.'

Same playbook as any stack, named in Rails terms. Interview stance: strongest in Go/Node, productive quickly in the others, fundamentals transfer.
